TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI
Agents with Distributed Information

Chanwoo Park    Jaywoong Jeong    Zachary Wojtowicz    Yubin Kim    Taekyun Lee    Kaiqing Zhang    Asuman Ozdaglar    MIT KAIST UT Austin University of Maryland⋆Equal contribution.
Abstract

Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team’s success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

1 Introduction

The frontier of AI is turning to multi-agent systems, in which AI agents are organized into teams that communicate to solve problems (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026a). Yet AI models are still trained and benchmarked largely as individual agents, which raises the question of whether they acquire the capacities and dispositions needed to be effective teammates. In human groups, collective intelligence, which is linked to social sensitivity and turn-taking, predicts team performance better than individual intelligence (Woolley et al., 2010). Although AI agents differ from humans, this finding motivates evaluating them as teams rather than only as individuals.

A central challenge in team decision-making is that decision-relevant information is typically distributed across members. Reaching a collective decision requires members to identify and retrieve relevant information, communicate it efficiently, and integrate it into a final decision. Team theory has long studied this challenge (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972), while empirical research on human group decision-making finds that people often struggle to identify and integrate critical private information (Stasser and Titus, 1985; Lu et al., 2012).

We introduce TeamGym, a gym for constructing team decision problem instances from source corpora, and for evaluating and training participant and coordinator policies under controlled information distributions and communication structures. TeamGym targets questions that existing benchmarks and multi-agent systems leave open. Single-agent benchmarks measure individual model capabilities (Wu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), while research on multi-agent LLM systems focuses on designing harnesses that solve a given problem (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026b). Neither offers much evidence on whether participants can retrieve and communicate decision-relevant information, how team performance varies with information distribution and communication structure, or whether training can improve participant and coordinator policies.

1.0.0.1 Method.

TeamGym constructs controlled team decision problem instances from real-world source corpora. For each instance, it derives a decision objective from one or more corpus questions and either retains a corpus-provided reference decision or constructs one from corpus annotations and source materials. Source annotations and reasoning associated with the reference decision guide the selection of candidate evidence units, such as sentences, paragraphs, tables, or code blocks. Source-specific grounding and model-based complete-set and leave-one-out checks retain units that together support the reference decision but whose individual removal leaves it unsupported or unresolved. These retained units are pivotal information units (PIUs) and collectively form the instance’s pivotal information.

Holding the problem instance and its pivotal information fixed, TeamGym can vary who initially has each PIU (the PIU distribution), whether participants receive PIUs directly or source material containing them, the communication structure, and token budgets. The team collectively receives the pivotal information, but the evidence is distributed across participants to make communication necessary for a fully supported final decision. The communication structure specifies whether a coordinator controls communication, how speakers are selected, and which decision maker makes the final decision. Token budgets constrain what decision makers may observe and generate. To understand what reduces team performance, we define two success-rate gaps. The communication gap is the drop when the same PIUs are distributed across participants rather than given to one model. The retrieval gap is the further drop when the team must retrieve those PIUs from source material rather than receive them directly. Beyond evaluation, TeamGym supports training participant and coordinator policies under controlled PIU distributions, communication structures, and token budgets.

We construct problem instances from source corpora in Table 1 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023b; Office of the Federal Register, 2026a; Office of the Federal Register, 2026b; Yu et al., 2027; Shen et al., 2022; Holzenberger et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Wisedocs, 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Raghavendra et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Source materials include contracts, regulations, SEC filings, biomedical papers, and source code, while the decision formats are finite-choice, written, and numeric.

1.0.0.2 Findings.

The resulting comparisons hold the problem instance and pivotal information fixed to isolate communication and retrieval effects from differences in problem difficulty. (1) Across eight language models and 12 source corpora, the decision success rate is 22.9 percentage points lower when the same PIUs are distributed across a team than when one model receives them all, and a further 19.9 points lower when the same team must retrieve its PIUs from source material rather than receiving them directly. (2) Across domains, differences in the success rate among communication structures vary across PIU-distribution conditions. For example, across the six legal source corpora when participants receive PIUs directly, sequential communication in which each speaker selects the next participant leads simultaneous communication by 3.9 points when one PIU is initially common to the team, but trails it by 9.8 points when the team includes an additional participant without a PIU, corresponding to a 13.8-point change in the difference between their success rates. (3) Optimizing final-decision quality changes the communication process itself. With coordinator control, joint two-policy training produces a compact, exhaustive information-elicitation protocol; without a coordinator, training the shared participant policy improves end-to-end final-decision quality and completion and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication. Tracing PIUs through these trajectories shows that increased participation makes more pivotal information available on FinDVer validation, but not on held-out FinLongDocQA.

TeamGym therefore provides a controlled environment in which team decision-making capabilities can be evaluated and trained under different information distributions and communication structures.

2 Related Work

2.0.0.1 Team decision theory and organizational economics.

Team decision theory studies cooperative decision makers with a team objective and a decentralized information structure. A team problem couples a shared objective with an information structure and one policy for each decision maker (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Yüksel and Başar, 2013). Classical analysis largely studies the properties of different computation structures and policies, not how they can be learned and implemented computationally. Under tractable joint-policy optimization (A1), computing this collection is assumed feasible before execution, although the exact problem can be intractable even in finite-horizon decentralized control (Bernstein et al., 2002). TeamGym instead evaluates and trains language-model policies, comparing policy collections before and after training under the same conditions.

2.0.0.2 Mechanism design.

Under the direct-report mechanism assumption (A2), mechanism design represents private information as a type that can be elicited directly under the applicable equilibrium assumptions, and that participants know their type and can communicate it if they so choose (Maskin and Sjostrom, 2002; Myerson, 1979; Myerson, 2008). In practice, however, attention and cognitive limitations constrain agent’s ability to identify, extract, and communicate information contained in long source material, even if it is in principle available to them (Mookherjee, 2006). TeamGym assumes a shared team payoff and studies bounded natural-language messages derived from source material.

2.0.0.3 Communication constraints.

Research in organizational economics, planning, and reinforcement learning examines communication costs and message limits (Cremer et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2024). The idealization of nonbinding communication resources (A3) permits decision makers to access and transmit relevant information without binding observation or message constraints. TeamGym instead makes its resource budgets explicit.

We defer additional related work on multistage communication, human-AI and group decision making, multi-agent LLM systems, benchmark contrasts, and the source corpora to Section 6.

3 TeamGym Environment

3.1 Decision Problem and Communication

We formalize TeamGym as a finite-horizon team decision problem (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Yüksel and Başar, 2013; Nayyar et al., 2013). A problem instance qq fixes underlying source materials, a decision objective, a decision format, a set 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} of possible final decisions, and a problem-specific evaluator that assigns each d∈𝒟qd\in\mathcal{D}_{q} a team payoff Uq​(d)∈[0,1]U_{q}(d)\in[0,1]. A decision maker is a role whose policy may generate a query, send a message, or make the final decision. A participant is a decision maker that may send messages during communication. A coordinator is a decision maker that may control communication by selecting or querying participants and may make the final decision. Initially, each participant receives an initial local observation, while all decision makers receive the same initial common observation containing the decision objective and decision format. The policy ρi\rho_{i} maps the information currently available to decision maker ii to a distribution over the queries, messages, or final decisions permitted for its role; ρ\rho denotes the collection of decision-maker policies. The communication structure 𝒞\mathcal{C} specifies whether a coordinator controls communication, which participants may send messages and when, whether messages are sequential or simultaneous, and which decision maker makes the final decision. The resource budgets BB, including token budgets, constrain what decision makers may observe and generate and how often participants may send messages. Queries and messages form the communication transcript; a decision maker’s local transcript is the portion available to it under 𝒞\mathcal{C} and BB. The initial local and common observations, together with the observation rules induced by 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the observation limits in BB, define the decentralized information structure. An episode is one complete execution through the final-decision stage for fixed qq, initial observations, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, BB, and ρ\rho. For these fixed inputs, the resulting interaction induces a distribution over final decisions, and we evaluate ρ\rho by its expected team payoff, 𝔼​[Uq​(d)]\mathbb{E}[U_{q}(d)]. Holding qq and the initial observations fixed while varying 𝒞\mathcal{C}, BB, or ρ\rho changes the interaction conditions without changing the problem instance.

For evaluation, we consider five communication structures (Figure 2), each proceeding in scheduled steps called communication rounds: (1) Round robin, under which one participant sends a message per round in a fixed cyclic order; (2) Current-speaker selection, which starts with the first participant in that order, after which each speaker selects the next participant; (3) Simultaneous responses, under which all participants respond in one round; (4) Coordinator-selected speaker, under which the coordinator selects and queries one participant per round; and (5) Broadcast query, under which the coordinator sends the same query to all participants, whose responses are generated in the same round. In Round robin, Current-speaker selection, and Simultaneous responses, no coordinator controls communication, and a separate final decision maker that does not participate in communication reads the complete communication transcript and makes the final decision. In Coordinator-selected speaker and Broadcast query, the coordinator controls communication and makes the final decision. Appendix C provides message-generation and implementation details and connections to prior work.

3.2 Problem-Instance Construction and Evaluation

TeamGym constructs each problem instance qq from one source corpus using materials such as contracts, SEC filings, biomedical papers, or source code. Each qq is paired with a reference decision drefd^{\mathrm{ref}} supported by its source materials and used in construction and evaluation. For each qq, we identify an inclusion-minimal set ℐqmin={i1,…,ik}\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\} called its pivotal information; each iji_{j} is a pivotal information unit (PIU). Informally, this information is sufficient to determine a final decision that achieves the highest possible team payoff, whereas removing any one PIU leaves insufficient information to guarantee such a decision. Because DeepSWE admits multiple valid patches and costly repository execution, it instead uses functional PIUs validated under a fixed, bounded protocol (Appendix D.6.4). Appendix D.1 formalizes this definition.

3.2.0.1 PIU construction.

When a model’s reasoning trace used to produce drefd^{\mathrm{ref}} is available, we retain it; otherwise, we generate reasoning conditioned on drefd^{\mathrm{ref}}, following answer-conditioned rationale generation (Wang et al., 2023a). To identify ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}, we use source annotations and the retained or generated reasoning to locate candidate units in the source materials. Grounding and model-based checks then test whether the candidates together support drefd^{\mathrm{ref}} and whether removing any one leaves the final decision unsupported or unresolved. The candidates retained by these checks form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}. We then verify that a model given all pivotal information can solve each evaluated problem instance (Section 4.1). Appendix D.7 reports an additional re-check of PIU necessity on representative instances using a model not used for construction.

3.2.0.2 PIU distribution.

A PIU distribution specifies who initially has each PIU in ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}: a PIU may be assigned to one or more participants through their initial local observations or placed in the initial common observation shared by the team. Figure 4 defines and illustrates five conditions. For a fixed qq, the conditions vary the PIU distribution while keeping the pivotal information and drefd^{\mathrm{ref}} unchanged. The initial common observation may also include participant descriptions, which summarize participants’ subject matter or function without revealing their assigned PIUs and can inform speaker selection.

3.2.0.3 Source-material distribution.

Rather than receiving PIUs directly, participants’ initial observations may contain portions of the contracts, filings, papers, or source code used to construct qq. We divide this source material into units without dividing a PIU, assign PIU-containing units according to the fixed PIU distribution, and distribute the remaining units across participants. For every problem instance, we then verify that no participant can produce a correct final decision from its initial local observation and the initial common observation. Appendix D.7 reports an additional re-check of this requirement on representative instances using a model not used for construction. Appendix D provides the formal source terminology and source-specific construction and distribution procedures.

3.2.0.4 Evaluation.

A problem family groups problem instances constructed from the same source corpus that require the same general kind of work and use the same evaluation procedure. For a problem family with a binary success criterion, episode success rate is the proportion of episodes whose final decisions succeed. Depending on the problem family, final decisions are compared with reference decisions or assessed by an LLM judge using problem-specific criteria. Software-engineering patches are checked by an official repository verifier.

4 Evaluation with TeamGym

We evaluate LLMs on problem instances constructed from legal, finance, medical, and software-engineering source corpora under three evaluation conditions: (1) Single-Agent All-PIU, in which one model receives all PIUs and makes the final decision; (2) Multi-Agent PIU-Only, in which the PIUs are distributed directly across participants; and (3) Multi-Agent Full-Context, in which the same participants instead receive source material containing their assigned PIUs. For each problem instance and LLM, the three conditions share the same PIUs and evaluator; the two multi-agent conditions also share the same PIU distribution, communication structure, and resource budgets.

Figure 5 summarizes how the information available to the decision maker changes across these three conditions and shows the corresponding aggregate communication and retrieval gaps.

4.1 Problem Instances

Table 1 summarizes the source corpora and decisions, while Table 2 reports the constructed and evaluated problem-instance counts. Before evaluation, we perform repeated checks in which GPT-5.5 receives all PIUs under Single-Agent All-PIU. It succeeds under the problem-specific evaluator at least once on every evaluated problem instance, verifying that a model given all pivotal information can solve the instance before the PIUs are distributed (Section 3.2). Appendix D reports additional construction details and problem-instance statistics for each source corpus.

4.2 Cross-Domain Communication and Retrieval Gaps

For this cross-domain comparison, both multi-agent conditions use One PIU per participant (Figure 4) and Coordinator-selected speaker. The communication gap is the decrease in episode success rate from Single-Agent All-PIU to Multi-Agent PIU-Only, and the retrieval gap is the additional decrease from Multi-Agent PIU-Only to Multi-Agent Full-Context. With the model and problem instance fixed, larger gaps indicate greater difficulty communicating and integrating distributed PIUs (communication gap) and retrieving them from source material (retrieval gap), rather than differences in model knowledge. The retrieval contrast corresponds to a departure from A2, and the communication contrast corresponds to a departure from A3. Figure 6 reports the episode success rates used to compute these gaps. Appendix E additionally reports Single-Agent Full-Context, in which one model receives all participants’ source material combined in participant order, removing team communication while retaining retrieval from source material.

Strong individual problem-solving does not guarantee effective teamwork: across all four domains, we observe substantial communication and retrieval gaps, although their magnitudes vary across domains and models. Single-Agent All-PIU reflects individual reasoning and decision-making capability when all pivotal information is directly available, but this individual performance does not by itself predict the model’s ability to communicate and integrate PIUs distributed across participants or to retrieve them from source material for team communication and integration.

4.3 Mechanisms Linking Communication Structure to Episode Success

Communication structure may affect episode success rate by changing the information supplied to the final decision maker. We examine two mechanisms through which access to earlier participant messages can change this input: correct synthesis and error uptake. Here, correct synthesis refers to an auditor-labeled, reference-supported inference that combines information. The intended criterion requires at least two distinct PIUs, but the current labels also include some inferences combining one PIU with information from the publicly visible decision options (Appendix E.4.2). Error uptake occurs when a later participant uses an incorrect or unsupported claim from an earlier visible message; rejecting or correcting that claim does not count.

We analyze Multi-Agent PIU-Only under One PIU per participant. In this setting, Round robin and Current-speaker selection achieve higher episode success rates than Simultaneous responses when the same Qwen3 model is used for the participants and the final decision maker. When only the final decision maker is replaced with GPT-5.5, however, the ordering reverses: Simultaneous responses achieves the highest rate. We use frozen participant trajectories to test how adding correct synthesis and removing error uptake affect episode success. A separate GPT-5.5 auditor labels sentence-level components. Participants are not rerun; we reconstruct the transcript input and regenerate only the final decision. Appendix E.4.1 reports the complete design and sample sizes. To isolate these mechanisms, we add correct synthesis while holding the PIUs supplied to the final decision maker fixed and excluding sentences that directly state a final choice or answer; separately, we remove only later sentences that use an earlier error while retaining the original error (Table 3).

Participant model Final decision maker Intervention effect (pp)
Add correct synthesis Remove error uptake
Qwen3-32B Same +14.6∗+14.6^{*} +2.5+2.5
GPT-5.5 +5.7∗+5.7^{*} +1.3+1.3
Qwen3-235B Same +17.7∗+17.7^{*} +5.7∗+5.7^{*}
GPT-5.5 +8.2∗+8.2^{*} +7.6∗+7.6^{*}

Access to earlier participant messages can improve decisions through correct synthesis or impair them through error uptake. The effects of both mechanisms depend in part on which model makes the final decision. Adding correct synthesis increases episode success rate in all four conditions, but replacing only the final decision maker with GPT-5.5 reduces its effect. Removing error uptake has a statistically significant effect only for Qwen3-235B participants, and its effect is smaller than the correct-synthesis effect in every condition. Appendix E.4 describes how correct synthesis and error uptake are identified and how each intervention is constructed.

4.4 PIU-Distribution and Communication-Structure Interaction

We evaluate this interaction across the 11 problem families for which we observe multiple PIU-distribution conditions and communication structures, testing whether the difference in episode success rate between communication structures changes across PIU-distribution conditions. DeepSWE is excluded because long-horizon repository execution and functional verification make this comparison computationally costly. Appendix F relates this comparison to team decision theory, communication complexity, and the hidden-profile paradigm in group decision-making.

We estimate separate logistic models for Multi-Agent PIU-Only and Multi-Agent Full-Context. For episode ee, let fef_{e}, mem_{e}, qeq_{e}, ℓe\ell_{e}, and cec_{e} denote the problem family, model, problem instance, PIU-distribution condition, and communication structure. We specify

ye∼Bernoulli⁡(pe),logit⁡(pe)=β0+γfe+αme+πℓe+λce+ωℓe,ce,y_{e}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{e}),\qquad\operatorname{logit}(p_{e})=\beta_{0}+\gamma_{f_{e}}+\alpha_{m_{e}}+\pi_{\ell_{e}}+\lambda_{c_{e}}+\omega_{\ell_{e},c_{e}},

where yey_{e} indicates episode success, pep_{e} is the probability of episode success, γfe\gamma_{f_{e}} and αme\alpha_{m_{e}} are problem-family and model fixed effects, πℓe\pi_{\ell_{e}} and λce\lambda_{c_{e}} are PIU-distribution and communication-structure terms, and ωℓe,ce\omega_{\ell_{e},c_{e}} is their interaction. One PIU per participant and Coordinator-selected speaker are the reference categories. We weight each episode by the inverse number of PIU-distribution conditions available for its problem instance qeq_{e}, so problem instances with more conditions do not receive greater aggregate weight, and cluster standard errors by problem instance.

Across the 11 included problem families and eight models, we reject the joint null that all PIU-distribution–communication-structure interaction terms are zero in both Multi-Agent PIU-Only (p<.001p<.001) and Multi-Agent Full-Context (p<.001p<.001). Thus, which communication structure performs better depends on the PIU distribution. Appendix Table 35 defines and reports the complete probability-scale interaction estimates, and Appendix E.6 reports the analysis with problem-instance fixed effects.

We examine two mechanisms in finance and SARA through matched comparisons and interventions; these do not estimate how much of the cross-domain regression interaction either mechanism explains.

4.4.1 Example 1: Narrow coordinator queries limit the PIUs communicated by one participant.

Across 59 finance problem instances, pooling Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B-A22B, the advantage of Round robin over Coordinator-selected speaker is larger under All-but-one PIU concentration: 31.4 percentage points, compared with 17.8 under One PIU per participant. The resulting +13.6+13.6-point interaction is statistically significant. Yet 99.2% of required participants speak in the concentrated condition. Under Coordinator-selected speaker, the selected participant receives a specific query. Its public description summarizes its subject matter or function without listing its assigned PIU categories, so the query may request only part of its evidence. Under Round robin, participants respond to the whole problem without a coordinator query. We therefore test whether broadening or removing the query reduces the communication-structure interaction when speaker selection is fixed.

We fix speaker selection, order, response count, private source material, and budgets. After selection, we append public PIU category labels that identify the topics of the selected participant’s assigned PIUs, with an instruction to report evidence for each category. The existing public participant description remains unchanged; the labels disclose no private facts, values, or answers. Messages and final decisions are regenerated.

We also replace the query with “It is your turn to contribute,” with and without the additions. Holding the original Round robin outcomes fixed, we recalculate the communication-structure interaction for each coordinator query condition. The original-query replay gives +15.5+15.5 points; Table 4 reports this 2×22\times 2 comparison.

Coordinator query Without labels or instruction With labels and instruction
Original coordinator query +15.5∗+15.5^{*} +5.9+5.9
Coordinator query removed −5.4-5.4 −9.3-9.3

Narrow coordinator queries contribute to the larger loss from PIU concentration under Coordinator-selected speaker. Adding the labels and instruction reduces the interaction from +15.5+15.5 to +5.9+5.9 points. Query removal changes it to −5.4-5.4 points without additions and −9.3-9.3 with them. All three changes from the original-query replay are statistically significant; none of the resulting interactions is significant. Both interventions selectively increase substantive PIU communication. These results support a role for query content, without establishing a zero residual interaction or separate effects of the labels and instruction. Appendix E.7.1–E.7.2 reports the design, success rates, and inference.

4.4.2 Example 2: Messages from participants assigned no PIU impair the final decision.

In the cross-domain Multi-Agent Full-Context regression, All-but-one PIU concentration shifts the comparison between Simultaneous responses and Coordinator-selected speaker by 4.0 percentage points toward the latter relative to One PIU per participant. This interaction is statistically significant. Source material could impair participants assigned PIUs or cause participants assigned no PIU to produce harmful messages. We examine these possibilities across 44 SARA problem instances, pooling Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, and GPT-5.5. We first compare Multi-Agent PIU-Only with a condition that adds the original private source material. In both conditions, participants receive their assigned PIUs explicitly as facts relevant to the decision; in Multi-Agent Full-Context, they must instead retrieve those facts from the source material. This comparison tests whether adding source material changes the interaction even when the relevant facts are already supplied directly. In Multi-Agent PIU-Only, the advantage of Simultaneous responses over Coordinator-selected speaker is 10.6 percentage points larger under All-but-one PIU concentration than under One PIU per participant. Adding source material changes this interaction to −5.1-5.1 points, a statistically significant change of −15.7-15.7 points.

To locate the loss, we next independently vary source-material access for participants assigned PIUs and those assigned no PIU, holding exact PIUs and public descriptions fixed. Under All-but-one PIU concentration and Simultaneous responses, source material only for participants assigned no PIU reduces episode success from 69.7% to 22.5%; source material only for participants assigned PIUs reduces it to 54.8%. The larger loss thus occurs without changing the latter group’s inputs. However, source placement changes both participant processing and messages, so it does not isolate their effect on the final decision.

If messages from participants assigned no PIU cause the loss, removing them should selectively improve success when their authors received source material. We therefore freeze all participant messages and regenerate only the final decision, comparing the complete transcript with one retaining only messages from participants assigned PIUs. Both transcript conditions regenerate the final decision, so the complete-transcript success rates differ slightly from those above. Table 5 reports this test. Table 5: Fixed-message intervention. Episode success rates under All-but-one PIU concentration and Simultaneous responses. Rows vary private source material for participants assigned no PIU; participants assigned PIUs receive no source material in either row. Effects are the change from removing messages, in pp. The interaction is the removal effect with source material minus that without it. Yellow cells and ∗ mark statistically significant effects. Source material Complete transcript Messages from participants assigned no PIU removed Effect (pp) Absent 69.9% 68.9% −1.0-1.0 Present 21.2% 68.9% +47.7∗+47.7^{*} Interaction +48.7∗+48.7^{*} Messages from participants assigned no PIU can impair the final decision, even when the evidence communicated by participants assigned PIUs is retained. Removing those messages improves success when their authors receive source material, with no statistically significant improvement when they do not. The interaction between source-material access and message removal is statistically significant. The result identifies a harmful contribution at the final-decision stage; it does not distinguish transcript length from distracting or contradictory content. Appendix E.7.3–E.7.4 reports the complete design, uncertainty estimates, and scope.

4.5 Token-Budget Effects

Under Multi-Agent Full-Context with One PIU per participant and Coordinator-selected speaker, we vary private-note, message, and local-transcript token budgets, which respectively limit unshared notes, messages, and newly available transcript text. Among them, the message budget has the strongest relationship with episode success rate: for GPT-5.5 on 24 CUAD and 29 Multi-LexSum instances, increasing it from 32 to 128 tokens raises the rate from 55.3% to 78.6%, averaged over private-note budgets, with no further gain at 256 tokens; private-note differences are smaller, and larger local-transcript budgets show no consistent improvement on Multi-LexSum. Appendix E.8 reports complete results and diagnostics.

5 Policy Training with TeamGym: Emergent Coordination

We demonstrate policy training with TeamGym under two communication structures: (1) Coordinator-selected speaker, where we train participant and coordinator policies and the coordinator selects and queries participants and makes the final decision; and (2) Current-speaker selection, where we train a shared participant policy and each current speaker either selects the next participant or ends communication. For this demonstration, the participant that ends communication makes the final decision, so no separate final decision maker is used. All policies are initialized from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024) and trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). In both demonstrations, the LLM-judged score assigned by GPT-5.5 serves as training reward. We call systematic changes in participation, speaker selection, and communication emergent coordination when these behaviors are not specified as separate rewards or training targets.

5.1 Coordinator-selected speaker: Training Participant and Coordinator

Under Coordinator-selected speaker, a shared participant policy generates messages from source material, while a coordinator policy generates queries and the final decision. We use Multi-Agent Full-Context on CUAD- and MAUD-derived problem instances (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023b), converting each decision task to a free-form written decision format while preserving its PIU distribution and source material (Appendix G.1.1). Training and checkpoint selection use only CUAD-derived problem instances; the 26 MAUD-derived problem instances evaluate transfer. We compare (1) two-stage policy training, which updates the participant and coordinator policies successively to examine which behaviors change when each policy is updated separately, and (2) joint two-policy training, which allows them to co-adapt and serves as the primary end-to-end experiment. Appendices G.1.2 and G.2 provide evaluation, optimization, and checkpoint-selection details.

5.1.1 Two-Stage Policy Training

On the 36 CUAD-derived validation instances, the LLM-judged score increases from 12.14% to 16.84% after the participant-only stage and to 23.33% after the coordinator-only continuation. Illustrative examples show that the participant-only stage changes which PIUs appear in participant messages and, through the resulting transcript, can change queries generated by the fixed coordinator policy; the coordinator-only continuation can change queries and final decisions even when participant messages remain substantively unchanged. Two-stage policy training can therefore change participant messages, coordinator queries, and final decisions, but its CUAD-derived validation gains do not transfer to the 26 held-out MAUD-derived problem instances. Appendix G.2.2 provides training details and illustrative examples.

5.1.2 Joint Two-Policy Training

Joint two-policy training produces short coordinator queries and queries every participant, despite not directly rewarding either behavior. On the 36 CUAD-derived validation problem instances, joint two-policy training increases the LLM-judged score from 11.97% to 22.38% and the share of problem instances in which the coordinator queries every participant from 80.6% to 100%. Because querying every participant does not enter the training reward, this increase is an instance of emergent coordination. Table 6 shows distinct coordinator-query behavior: joint two-policy training uses shorter queries, queries every participant, and never copies the problem question in the first query, whereas two-stage policy training uses longer queries and more later queries that reuse terms from preceding participant replies. Figure 7(a) reports the scheduled validation trajectory.

On 26 MAUD-derived instances, under joint two-policy training the coordinator queries every participant and every participant sends a public message in all 26, versus 20 under the base policies, while the aggregate LLM-judged score changes only from 5.12% to 5.58%. Thus, coordination behavior transfers even when final-decision quality changes little. Appendix G.2.3 provides training details, an example, and additional analyses.

5.2 Current-speaker selection: Training a Shared Participant Policy

We train a shared participant policy under Current-speaker selection in Multi-Agent PIU-Only with One PIU per participant. The shared policy controls participant messages, next-participant selection, decisions to end communication, and the final decision. Public participant descriptions are visible to support participant selection. Training uses 350 FinDVer problem instances and 188 two- or three-participant FinLongDocQA problem instances. We select the checkpoint using the 39-instance FinDVer validation subset and report separate evaluations on the 21-instance FinLongDocQA validation subset and 40 held-out four-participant FinLongDocQA problem instances. The held-out test comparison therefore asks whether a policy trained on two- and three-participant FinLongDocQA problem instances also improves performance on four-participant instances. The trained shared participant policy improves LLM-judged scores on both validation subsets and on held-out four-participant FinLongDocQA problem instances. Figure 7(b) and Table 7 report the results. Appendix G.3 provides the data-split, optimization, checkpoint-selection, and diagnostic details.

Here, a communication trajectory comprises the communication transcript, next-participant selections, the decision to end communication, and the identity and assigned PIU of the participant making the final decision. The final-decision policy is the base or trained shared participant policy used only to regenerate the final decision. Cross-replay holds this trajectory and the final-decision prompt fixed while varying the final-decision policy. Across these 40 problem instances, replacing the base communication trajectory with the trained trajectory, averaged across the two final-decision policies, yields a 6.95-point gain. Replacing the base final-decision policy with the trained policy does not produce a statistically significant improvement. Thus, within cross-replay, the validation gain is concentrated in the communication trajectory rather than the final-decision policy. Training also increases the proportion of participants who send public messages and the number of distinct speakers while reducing the rate at which a speaker selects itself as the next participant on validation and test. Because these diagnostics do not enter the reward, the changes provide evidence of emergent coordination in participation and next-participant selection.

To test whether additional public messages make more PIUs available for the final decision, we apply the same GPT-5.5 final-decision policy to every base and trained communication transcript. Unlike cross-replay, this analysis retains every trajectory, including valid public messages produced before an episode that does not reach a final decision. On FinDVer, trained transcripts improve performance under the same final-decision policy by 12.6 points and increase the proportion of PIUs appearing in the transcript by 15.9 points. On held-out FinLongDocQA, however, end-to-end score and final-decision completion improve, but the changes in performance under the same final-decision policy and in the proportion of PIUs appearing in the transcript are not statistically distinguishable from zero. Together, these results show that broader participation and higher end-to-end performance do not necessarily coincide with a larger proportion of PIUs appearing in the communication transcript. Table 10 reports these comparisons, and Appendix G.3.5 reports additional diagnostics.

Across both fixed communication structures, training changes unrewarded coordination behaviors as well as final-decision quality. Under Coordinator-selected speaker, the participant and coordinator policies change participant messages, coordinator queries, and final decisions; under Current-speaker selection, the shared participant policy changes participation, next-participant selection, and the communication trajectory. Each demonstration reports one training run; results across additional runs and base models remain to be evaluated.

6 Additional Related Work

6.0.0.1 Mechanism design and communication.

Multistage communication games, communication equilibria, and communication requirements study communication before a decision (Myerson, 1986; Forges, 1986; Segal, 2007). Cheap-talk models instead study communication with preference misalignment (Crawford and Sobel, 1982).

6.0.0.2 Human-AI and group decision making.

Human-AI decision making motivates evaluating AI systems as team participants and examining the interaction process rather than only the final decision (Lai et al., 2021; Herath Pathirannehelage et al., 2025; Seeber et al., 2020). Hidden-profile studies show that human teams can fail to reveal uniquely held information, and collective-intelligence research relates interaction structure to performance (Stasser and Titus, 1985; Woolley et al., 2010). Work on limited attention, working memory, and information overload motivates finite resource constraints (Kahneman, 1973; Cowan, 2001; Eppler and Mengis, 2004). These findings motivate our controlled comparisons, but TeamGym does not evaluate human-AI teams or treat its token budgets as models of human cognition. Work using LLMs to simulate social settings has a different objective: plausible social behavior is the object of study, whereas TeamGym treats the participant model as a controlled component (Park et al., 2022; Park et al., 2023; Hansen et al., 2026).

6.0.0.3 Multi-agent LLM systems and benchmark contrasts.

CAMEL, AutoGen, MetaGPT, and ChatDev study collaboration through prompted agent interaction (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024). PEER learns collaborative writing, MDAgents studies adaptive medical collaboration, and other work studies debate and collaborative post-training (Schick et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025). CooperBench evaluates cooperative coding over repositories (Khatua et al., 2026). These systems study agent coordination, but TeamGym fixes source-grounded PIUs, controls the PIU distribution and whether participants receive PIUs directly or source material containing them, and measures whether bounded communication makes the PIUs available for a final decision. Multi-agent debate commonly gives agents the same problem; TeamGym gives participants different initial local observations.

MultiAgentBench evaluates coordination under several communication topologies (Zhu et al., 2025). HiddenBench evaluates whether teams surface and combine directly presented hidden facts (Li et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026), while SILO-BENCH studies role-free collaboration on synthetic distributed-computation problems (Zhang et al., 2026). Appendix B gives compact comparisons with both benchmarks. Collaborative Gym studies a user or user simulator collaborating with one LLM agent, while our unit of analysis is a team with decision-relevant evidence divided among participants (Shao et al., 2026). Single-agent suites such as SmartPlay and AgentBench do not require recovery of evidence held by teammates (Wu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024).

The original evaluations for the finance, medical, and software-engineering source corpora in Table 1 are single-agent or centralized. FinDVer and FinLongDocQA study financial verification and long-document financial question answering (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026); MLCR and EvidenceBench provide long medical-record cases and hypothesis-linked biomedical evidence (Wisedocs, 2026; Wang et al., 2025); and SWE Atlas Codebase QnA studies repository comprehension (Raghavendra et al., 2026). TeamGym uses the evaluated source corpora to construct team decision problem instances with controlled PIU distributions.

7 Conclusion

We introduce TeamGym, a gym for constructing team decision problem instances and for evaluating and training participant and coordinator policies under controlled PIU distributions, communication structures, and token budgets. Across 8 language models and 12 source corpora, distributing the same PIUs across participants reduces episode success rate by 22.9 percentage points relative to providing them to a single model, and requiring participants to retrieve those PIUs from source material reduces it by a further 19.9 points. The effectiveness of a communication structure also varies across PIU-distribution conditions. Team decision-making therefore depends not only on individual model capabilities, but also on how participants retrieve, communicate, and integrate distributed information.

Across two fixed communication structures, policy training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication. With coordinator control, joint two-policy training produces a compact information-elicitation protocol; without a coordinator, training improves end-to-end final-decision quality and completion while increasing participation. Tracing PIUs through these trajectories shows that increased participation makes more pivotal information available on FinDVer validation, but not on held-out FinLongDocQA. This distinction illustrates how TeamGym diagnoses how training changes team decision making, rather than reporting only whether performance improves.

These training demonstrations use one run each, and the improvements under Coordinator-selected speaker are measured on CUAD-derived validation problem instances used for checkpoint selection. On MAUD-derived problem instances, the learned query and messaging patterns transfer more clearly than final-decision quality. Extensions of TeamGym could relax the shared-payoff assumption to study strategic information transmission, malicious or unreliable participants, and teams with partially aligned objectives. They could also introduce explicit retrieval costs and allow participants to choose which source material to retrieve. By separating retrieval, communication, and final decisions while holding the underlying problem fixed, TeamGym provides a controlled foundation for diagnosing and training team decision-making capabilities.

Reproducibility Statement

The supplementary material documents the problem-instance construction procedures, evaluation settings, prompts and evaluator protocols, statistical analyses, and policy-training configurations and diagnostic analyses (Appendices D, C, E, E.8, G.1.2, G.2, and G.3). The forthcoming supplementary archive will provide the code, configurations, dataset-access and preparation instructions, prompts, and generated artifacts needed to reproduce all reported problem-instance construction, evaluation, analysis, and policy-training results. The code will be released soon.

Use of AI Assistants

The authors used OpenAI Codex for code development and manuscript editing. For the legal, finance, medical, and software-engineering environment, language models were also used within the research methodology for problem-instance construction and semantic evaluation, as described in the corresponding construction and evaluation sections. These uses include generating reasoning during problem-instance construction when it was not provided, proposing and checking problem annotations, and judging candidate final decisions against reference decisions. The authors designed these procedures, reviewed their outputs, and developed and approved all scientific claims in the final paper.

Appendix B Closest Benchmark Comparisons

B.0.0.1 HiddenBench.

HiddenBench is the closest benchmark to TeamGym because both study team decisions under decentralized information structures. HiddenBench provides broad coverage of Hidden Profile settings (Version 4 evaluates 65 problem instances and 15 models) and examines whether directly presented participant-specific facts enter public discussion and improve group voting (Li et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). TeamGym complements this breadth by treating the source-grounded information and interaction environment as controlled experimental variables: it varies PIU distribution, whether participants receive PIUs directly or source material containing them, communication structure, and token budgets while holding the underlying problem and evidence requirements fixed. Paired contrasts and PIU-distribution–communication-structure regressions quantify how performance changes across these conditions, while PIU-level process tracing localizes plausible stages at which required evidence is lost. TeamGym additionally supports a participant-only stage, a coordinator-only continuation, and joint two-policy training under Coordinator-selected speaker, together with training of a shared participant policy under Current-speaker selection, with the participant that ends communication making the final decision. Thus, HiddenBench provides a broader Hidden Profile evaluation, whereas TeamGym provides a more controlled, source-grounded environment for studying how PIU distribution and communication structure jointly relate to team performance.

B.0.0.2 SILO-BENCH.

SILO-BENCH studies role-free agents solving synthetic distributed-computation problems under direct-message, broadcast, and shared-file protocols, with programmatically known answers and weak-scaling evaluations from 2 to 100 agents (Zhang et al., 2026). This design is particularly useful for examining how emergent organization, consensus, and communication cost change as both team size and the global problem grow. TeamGym instead holds each real-world decision problem and its evidence requirements fixed while varying PIU distribution, whether participants receive PIUs directly or source material containing them, communication structure, and token budgets. Its communication gap compares Single-Agent All-PIU with Multi-Agent PIU-Only, while its retrieval gap compares Multi-Agent PIU-Only with Multi-Agent Full-Context. These outcome-based contrasts are distinct from SILO-BENCH’s log-based Communication-Reasoning Gap. TeamGym also supports a participant-only stage, a coordinator-only continuation, and joint two-policy training under Coordinator-selected speaker, together with training of a shared participant policy under Current-speaker selection, with the participant that ends communication making the final decision. Consequently, SILO-BENCH characterizes how emergent collaboration behaves under weak scaling, whereas TeamGym more directly examines how controlled PIU distributions and communication structures relate to performance on fixed, source-grounded team decisions.

Appendix C Communication-Structure Implementation and Relation to Prior Work

C.0.0.1 Message generation and structure-specific implementation.

At each communication round, the environment constructs the current observation permitted by the communication structure and resource budgets. The applicable participant or coordinator policy receives this observation and generates an action permitted for its role, such as a participant message, coordinator query and speaker selection, or final decision. The implementation uses role-specific prompt templates and structured output schemas, parses the returned action, and applies structure-specific fallback rules. Model and decoding settings are reported with the corresponding evaluation or training setup. Under Current-speaker selection, an omitted or invalid next-participant selection defaults to the next participant in the fixed cyclic order.

C.0.0.2 Relation to prior work.

The three structures without coordinator control are related to public deliberation and multi-agent debate (Gerardi and Yariv, 2007; Du et al., 2024), whereas the two coordinator-controlled structures are related to mediated communication and fusion-center models (Myerson, 1986; Forges, 1986; Varshney, 1997). Their speaker-selection rules also draw on mechanisms studied in conversation analysis and multi-agent systems (Sacks et al., 1974; Wu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2019). The five structures are not intended as an exhaustive taxonomy of communication structures.

Appendix D Problem-Instance Construction and Statistics

We report source-specific construction choices, checks, and problem-instance statistics for the legal, finance, medical, and software-engineering source corpora. Sections 3.1–3.2 define the terminology and general construction requirements; here we provide implementation details and source-specific statistics.

D.0.0.1 Source terminology.
  • •

    A source corpus is the collection of records, annotations, or other artifacts from which problem instances are constructed.

  • •

    The underlying source materials for a problem instance qq are the particular records or artifacts selected from its source corpus.

  • •

    Source material denotes the portions of the underlying source materials placed in participants’ initial observations.

D.1 Decision Sufficiency and Pivotal Information

For a problem instance qq and an evidence subset SS, let vq​(S)v_{q}(S) denote the corresponding information view: the decision objective, decision format, any other fixed public information, and the evidence in SS. The view excludes omitted source information, the reference decision, evaluator-side annotations, and other hidden construction metadata.

Let 𝒬q\mathcal{Q}_{q} be a comparison class containing qq and other admissible problem instances that preserve qq’s public decision specification and set 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} of possible final decisions. Admissibility is defined relative to the problem family: an admissible instance must satisfy the same domain constraints and evaluation rule while potentially differing in information not contained in the given view. For an information view vv, define

Ωq​(v)={q~∈𝒬q:q~​ is consistent with ​v}.\Omega_{q}(v)=\left\{\widetilde{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{q}:\widetilde{q}\text{ is consistent with }v\right\}.

Thus, the information in vv does not distinguish qq from the other instances in Ωq​(v)\Omega_{q}(v).

For each q~∈𝒬q\widetilde{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{q}, let

𝒟q~⋆=arg⁡maxd∈𝒟q​Uq~​(d)\mathcal{D}_{\widetilde{q}}^{\star}=\arg\max_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{q}}U_{\widetilde{q}}(d)

be its set of optimal final decisions. We call SS decision-sufficient for qq if

⋂q~∈Ωq​(vq​(S))𝒟q~⋆≠∅.\bigcap_{\widetilde{q}\in\Omega_{q}(v_{q}(S))}\mathcal{D}_{\widetilde{q}}^{\star}\neq\varnothing.

Equivalently, the information view identifies at least one final decision that is optimal for every admissible problem instance consistent with that view.

We call ℐqmin={i1,…,ik}\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\} the pivotal information for qq, and each ij∈ℐqmini_{j}\in\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q} a pivotal information unit (PIU), if

⋂q~∈Ωq​(vq​(ℐqmin))𝒟q~⋆≠∅\bigcap_{\widetilde{q}\in\Omega_{q}(v_{q}(\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}))}\mathcal{D}_{\widetilde{q}}^{\star}\neq\varnothing

and, for every ij∈ℐqmini_{j}\in\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q},

⋂q~∈Ωq​(vq​(ℐqmin∖{ij}))𝒟q~⋆=∅.\bigcap_{\widetilde{q}\in\Omega_{q}(v_{q}(\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}\setminus\{i_{j}\}))}\mathcal{D}_{\widetilde{q}}^{\star}=\varnothing.

The pivotal information therefore identifies a common optimal decision, whereas after removing any PIU, no final decision is guaranteed to be optimal across all admissible instances consistent with the remaining information.

The construction procedure does not enumerate Ωq​(vq​(S))\Omega_{q}(v_{q}(S)). Instead, it operationalizes the complete-set and leave-one-out conditions using source annotations, reference reasoning, grounding checks, and model-based sufficiency checks. The resulting ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q} need not be unique: another inclusion-minimal evidence set may also identify the decision. Separately, the centralized checks under Single-Agent All-PIU test whether the reference decision can be produced from the selected pivotal information.

D.2 General Construction Procedure

D.2.0.1 Reference decisions and reasoning.

Each problem instance is constructed from one or more source questions; the decision objective may retain one question or combine related questions. When a reference decision and the reasoning used to produce it accompany the source questions, we retain them. Otherwise, we construct the reference decision from the available source annotations and underlying source materials. When the reasoning is unavailable, we generate reasoning conditioned on the reference decision; answer-conditioned rationale generation provides one example of this procedure (Wang et al., 2023a).

D.2.0.2 Candidate-unit and removal checks.

The fixed decision objective, reference decision, and reasoning used to produce it identify the information in the underlying source materials that supports the required answer components or reasoning steps. Dividing this information into candidate units is source-specific; a candidate unit may be a sentence, paragraph, or code block. The construction procedure requires each retained candidate unit to be necessary for at least one required answer component or reasoning step. When the retained or generated reasoning does not establish whether this requirement holds, a model-based check using a model such as GPT-5.5 first requires the model to produce the reference decision. The procedure then removes one candidate unit at a time and asks whether uncertainty remains about the reference decision given the decision objective and remaining units. The removed unit is retained when uncertainty remains and excluded otherwise. This process continues until removing any retained unit leaves uncertainty about the reference decision; the retained units form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}. When necessity is established from the retained or generated reasoning, the released construction code also provides the model-based removal check as an additional check.

D.2.0.3 PIU and source-material distribution.

For Pairwise PIU overlap, we use a seeded random ordering to assign PIUs to the participant positions defined by the condition. Appendix D.3.8.5 reports an additional Multi-LexSum analysis that orders PIUs using embedding-based similarity while preserving the condition. After the PIU distribution is fixed, the underlying source materials are divided into units without dividing a PIU. Units that do not contain a PIU are distributed across participants using source-specific procedures that may account for their distance from a participant’s PIUs and balance the lengths of participants’ initial local observations. Afterward, we verify each participant’s initial local observation together with the initial common observation and, when necessary and consistent with the source, truncate the material. For example, legal source materials may be truncated, whereas source code is not truncated when doing so would prevent the program from functioning.

D.2.0.4 Participant identifiers and participant descriptions.

A participant description is a prompt-visible phrase describing a participant’s subject matter or function without disclosing the specific content, values, or conclusions of the PIUs assigned to that participant. Participant identifiers and participant descriptions disclosed to every decision maker form part of the initial common observation. Because participant descriptions indicate which participant is likely to hold relevant information, decision makers can use them to inform speaker selection. Participant descriptions do not determine the structural roles of participant, coordinator, or separate final decision maker defined in Section 3.1. The source-specific procedures below describe their construction and leakage checks.

D.3 Legal

Table 11 summarizes the six legal problem families and their source corpora.

D.3.1 Common Legal Construction Procedure

D.3.1.1 Step 1. Select the underlying source materials.

A problem instance draws from exactly one contract, agreement, transaction specification, case file, litigation collection, or tax case, according to its source corpus.

D.3.1.2 Step 2. Specify the decision objective and format.

For CUAD and MAUD, a construction model uses one or more questions and their grounded excerpts from the source corpus to construct a new finite-choice legal-review question and reference decision. It constructs a decision set 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} of mutually exclusive, legally plausible alternatives with comparable specificity. The other alternatives have similar complexity to the reference decision, and the alternatives are written as natural legal profiles rather than explicit sums of answer components. For CUAD and MAUD, the grounded excerpts used to support the reference decision are candidate units. The other four source corpora use written or numeric final decisions. Construction uses the reference decision and the reasoning used to produce it to identify candidate units in the underlying source materials. The source-specific procedures below determine which candidate units form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}.

D.3.1.3 Step 3. Identify the pivotal information.

We apply the PIU construction requirements in Section 3.2. If the checks identify multiple inclusion-minimal sets that satisfy these requirements, CUAD and MAUD retain one as the pivotal information before constructing the PIU distribution. eCFR Casebook, MSLR, and Multi-LexSum identify the pivotal information directly from units needed for distinct reasoning steps.

D.3.1.4 Step 4. Define the PIU distribution.

We apply the PIU-distribution conditions in Figure 4 subject to the construction requirements in Section 3.2. Some conditions are ineligible for problem instances with only two PIUs; we do not add artificial PIUs to force a condition.

D.3.1.5 Step 5. Construct participant descriptions.

Each participant receives a participant description based on the PIUs assigned to that participant and not included in the initial common observation. For each PIU, a construction model produces a short phrase describing its broad subject or function. The phrase must not disclose the PIU’s specific content, values, conclusions, or effect on the final decision. The phrases corresponding to the PIUs assigned to a participant are combined deterministically to form the participant description for that participant. A participant assigned no PIU outside the initial common observation receives the participant description context reviewer, followed by the participant number. The participant descriptions form part of the initial common observation. For eCFR Casebook, MSLR, Multi-LexSum, and SARA, a separate model-based check assesses this requirement, and descriptions that fail the check are revised.

D.3.1.6 Step 6. Check initial observations and complete problem-instance construction.

We apply the participant-level source-material check in Section 3.2. Removable non-PIU information that permits one participant to produce the correct final decision alone is deleted and the check is repeated; a problem instance is rejected if such information cannot be removed. Finite-choice labels are permuted after construction to prevent position regularities.

D.3.2 Problem Instances and PIU Distributions in the Legal Evaluation

The legal model comparison evaluates the same 163 retained problem instances under the three evaluation conditions. Because CUAD and MAUD contain substantially more retained problem instances than the other legal source corpora, we use 30 problem instances from each, with at most one problem instance per contract or agreement. For eCFR Casebook, MSLR, Multi-LexSum, and SARA, we use every retained problem instance. Each problem instance uses the One PIU per participant condition in the two team conditions.

The PIU-distribution–communication-structure evaluation uses 514 PIU distributions under the five PIU-distribution conditions in Figure 4. For each of the eight models, the evaluation design crosses each PIU distribution with the five communication structures in Figure 2 under Multi-Agent PIU-Only and Multi-Agent Full-Context.

D.3.3 Legal Problem-Instance and PIU-Distribution Statistics

Figure 8 reports the PIU count and PIU length for the 163 problem instances in the legal evaluation. It also reports participant count and the length of source material provided to participants for the 514 PIU distributions under the five PIU-distribution conditions in Figure 4. For the first two measures, each point is one problem instance; for the latter two, each point is one PIU distribution.

Source-material length sums the material provided to each participant after applying the initial-local-observation token budget of 40,000 tokens. Repeated material is counted for each participant who receives it because it contributes separately to that participant’s retrieval burden. PIU length is measured from the PIU text supplied in Multi-Agent PIU-Only. All lengths use the same cl100k_base tokenizer used for initial-local-observation budgeting. Table 12 reports the corresponding means; measures that depend on PIU distribution are first averaged within problem instance and then across problem instances.

D.3.4 CUAD Problem-Instance Construction

D.3.4.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

CUAD (Hendrycks et al., 2021) provides contract-level annotations across commercial clause categories. We do not use the original CUAD label as the final decision. A question such as “does this contract contain source-code escrow?” does not require multiple PIUs because one annotated span can determine the final decision. Instead, we use contract–label pairs with two to five positive annotated spans to construct finite-choice problem instances. Contract–label pairs with negative labels are excluded because the decision objective requires combining information rather than proving absence from a long contract.

The construction procedure produces 542 candidate problem instances. Of these, 539 admit at least one PIU distribution under the conditions in Figure 4, and 538 are retained after the common legal checks and the CUAD-specific checks below. The 538 retained problem instances, which are reported as the constructed CUAD problem instances in Table 2, are drawn from 289 distinct contracts. Most retained problem instances (514) contain two PIUs; the remaining 24 contain at least three. For the legal model comparison, we use the first retained problem instance from each previously unseen contract in the released order until 30 contracts are represented.

D.3.4.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

For each eligible contract–label pair, a construction model selects positive annotated spans and constructs a finite-choice problem instance whose final decision depends on their content.

Each candidate unit is one CUAD-annotated span. If a span contains several legal facts, they remain within one candidate unit; if two spans express similar legal content, they remain separate candidate units.

Using the selected candidate units, construction follows the common legal procedure in Appendix D.3 to construct the question, decision set, and reference decision. The alternatives use neutral, opaque identifiers, with their legal content placed in their definitions. The model-based check in Section 3.2 determines which candidate units form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}. Because CUAD problem instances use a finite-choice decision format, each constructed problem instance must admit exactly one reference decision. Ambiguous questions such as “is this clause risky?” or “is this protection good enough?” are rejected unless the alternatives are specified so that the problem instance admits one reference decision.

Table 13 summarizes the CUAD label families used in construction.

D.3.4.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

For CUAD, the underlying source material is the source contract, rather than only the annotated spans that determine the reference decision. The source contract is divided into contiguous units using legal section headings first, then paragraphs, sentences, and words as progressively weaker split points. A unit does not divide a PIU. Units containing PIUs are provided to the participants assigned those PIUs under the PIU distribution.

Units that do not contain a PIU are distributed based on their overlap with participant descriptions and PIUs, their proximity to PIUs in the source contract, their legal section, and the lengths of participants’ initial local observations. A unit with overlap or proximity to a PIU is, when possible, provided to a participant not assigned that PIU.

D.3.4.4 Example participant descriptions.

The CUAD label is not provided to participants. Table 14 provides example participant descriptions constructed under the common legal procedure.

D.3.4.5 CUAD-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common legal checks in Appendix D.3, CUAD requires each candidate unit to be a positive annotated span copied exactly from the source contract with a recoverable source location. Each problem instance must contain at least two PIUs. The units used to divide the source contract must collectively cover it without dividing a PIU. A problem instance is rejected if it fails any of these checks.

D.3.5 MAUD Problem-Instance Construction

D.3.5.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

MAUD (Wang et al., 2023b) pairs merger agreements with expert-curated annotations of their provisions. The source corpus contains 25,827 annotation rows from 153 agreements. Construction uses 100 agreements and produces 557 retained problem instances from 318 agreement–category pairs. Of those pairs, 239 produce two problem instances and 79 produce one. Among the 557 retained problem instances, 178 contain two PIUs and 379 contain at least three. The legal evaluation uses 30 fixed problem instances from distinct agreements, as described in Appendix D.3.2.

The source corpus organizes annotation rows under seven legal categories. The retained problem instances use the four categories in Table 15.

D.3.5.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Many MAUD row-level questions can be answered from one provision excerpt. We therefore use the annotated questions and excerpts to construct a finite-choice problem instance whose final decision depends on multiple provisions from the same agreement and category. The alternatives describe the combined legal profile implied by those provisions rather than reproduce the MAUD row-level annotations.

A MAUD row may contain a curated provision excerpt rather than a complete agreement section, and some rows join passages separated by omitted text. Construction removes annotation artifacts, divides such rows at omitted-text markers, and does not reconstruct omitted text. Each resulting provision excerpt is a candidate unit. Construction then locates the candidate unit in the agreement, using exact matching when possible and normalization when necessary. The model-based check in Section 3.2 determines which candidate units form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}. The MAUD row-level annotation is used to organize candidate units but is not itself a PIU.

D.3.5.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

For MAUD, the underlying source material is the merger agreement. The agreement is divided into contiguous units without dividing a PIU. Units containing PIUs are provided to the participants assigned those PIUs under the PIU distribution. The remaining units are distributed based on their overlap with participant descriptions and PIUs, their proximity to PIUs in the agreement, their legal section, and the lengths of participants’ initial local observations. When an initial local observation is truncated under the applicable resource budget, every PIU assigned to that participant remains present.

D.3.5.4 MAUD-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common legal checks in Appendix D.3, MAUD requires every PIU to be a provision excerpt from a source annotation row and to have a recoverable location in the agreement. Each problem instance must contain at least two PIUs from one agreement and one retained category. The units used to divide the agreement must preserve every PIU. A problem instance is rejected if it fails any of these checks.

D.3.6 eCFR Casebook Problem-Instance Construction

D.3.6.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

eCFR Casebook uses regulatory text from 12 C.F.R. Parts 1 and 3 together with controlled transaction memos (Office of the Federal Register, 2026a; Office of the Federal Register, 2026b; Office of the Federal Register, 2026c). The regulatory text covers bank investment securities and related capital requirements. Each transaction memo states the facts needed to apply one or more of these provisions. Construction produces 20 candidate problem instances. Eighteen are retained after the common legal checks and the eCFR Casebook-specific checks below. The legal evaluation uses all 18 retained problem instances.

D.3.6.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Each problem instance asks for a short written compliance conclusion about one transaction memo. The final decision must state the controlling regulatory status or rule, the relevant transaction facts, any required threshold, exception, or calculation, and the resulting action. These requirements form the answer components evaluated in the final decision. The evaluator for free-form decisions in Appendix G.1.2 compares the final decision with the reference decision and these answer components.

Construction selects regulatory provisions whose application depends on more than one condition. Candidate units consist of regulatory text copied from the eCFR and transaction facts copied from the memo. The model-based check in Section 3.2 determines which candidate units form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}. The retained problem instances contain five to seven PIUs.

D.3.6.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

For eCFR Casebook, the underlying source materials are the eCFR provisions and the transaction memo. These materials are divided into long excerpts without dividing a PIU. Each excerpt containing a PIU is provided to a participant assigned that PIU under the PIU distribution, and PIUs assigned to other participants are removed from that participant’s source material. Each participant’s source material has a target length of 12,000 tokens; across the retained problem instances, the resulting lengths range from 9,846 to 11,830 tokens.

D.3.6.4 eCFR Casebook-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common legal checks in Appendix D.3, eCFR Casebook requires every PIU to occur in the regulatory text or transaction memo. Construction checks that each PIU appears in the initial local observation of every participant assigned that PIU and not in the initial local observations of participants not assigned that PIU. A retained problem instance must also pass the model-based solvability check with all PIUs centralized. A problem instance is rejected if it fails any of these checks.

D.3.7 MSLR Problem-Instance Construction

D.3.7.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

MSLR (Yu et al., 2027) provides anonymized Chinese administrative-enforcement case files. The source corpus used in construction contains 1,389 case files, of which 613 identify one target party, contain the required source material, and state a final judgment. Construction selects 100 candidate problem instances. After the common legal checks and the MSLR-specific checks below, 11 problem instances are retained. The legal evaluation uses all 11 retained problem instances.

D.3.7.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Each problem instance asks for a short written enforcement conclusion for one target party. The reference decision combines the material nonpublic information and its timing, the basis for the party’s knowledge or access, the party’s trading conduct, the legal characterization, and the final administrative handling. The final judgment supplies the final administrative handling. These requirements form the answer components evaluated in the final decision. The evaluator for free-form decisions in Appendix G.1.2 compares the final decision with the reference decision and these answer components.

Construction identifies six exact, nonoverlapping excerpts from the case file. The excerpts cover the event and timing, knowledge or access, trading conduct, legal characterization, and final handling. Each candidate unit retains its location in the case file. We apply the PIU construction requirements in Section 3.2; every retained MSLR problem instance contains six PIUs.

D.3.7.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

For MSLR, the underlying source material is the complete anonymized case file. Each participant receives the case file with the exact excerpts corresponding to the PIUs assigned to that participant. Passages corresponding to PIUs not assigned to that participant are removed before the source material is provided.

D.3.7.4 MSLR-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common legal checks in Appendix D.3, MSLR requires each problem instance to identify one target party and to contain a final judgment. Every candidate unit must be copied exactly from the case file, have a recoverable source location, and not overlap another candidate unit. A retained problem instance must also pass the model-based solvability check with all PIUs centralized. A problem instance is rejected if it fails any of these checks.

D.3.8 Multi-LexSum Problem-Instance Construction

D.3.8.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

Multi-LexSum (Shen et al., 2022) contains 4,539 civil-litigation collections.
