Of these, 3,086 contain between three and 18 source documents and have a Multi-LexSum summary within the length range used in construction. A model-based check of source grounding retains 48 candidate problem instances, and construction selects 30 for the remaining checks. After the common legal checks and the Multi-LexSum-specific checks below, 29 problem instances are retained. The legal evaluation uses all 29 retained problem instances.

D.3.8.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Each problem instance asks for a written procedural or legal conclusion that requires two to four interdependent conclusions from the documents in one litigation collection. The question and reference decision are based on the original documents rather than the Multi-LexSum summary. Construction removes from the question the names and source-specific identifiers that would identify the litigation collection. The evaluator for free-form decisions in Appendix G.1.2 compares the final decision with the reference decision and the required answer components.

Construction identifies decision-relevant information in the original documents and states each candidate unit concisely. Each candidate unit records the sentence identifiers in the original documents that support it. Each candidate unit must distinguish the reference decision from at least one alternative considered during construction. We apply the PIU construction requirements in Section 3.2.

A model-based check compares each candidate unit with the supporting sentences and requires the original documents to support the complete reference decision. Each retained problem instance contains eight to twelve PIUs.

D.3.8.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

For Multi-LexSum, the underlying source materials are the original documents in one litigation collection. The source material provided to a participant contains the original-document sentences supporting each PIU assigned to that participant, together with additional passages from the same litigation collection. Units containing PIUs and units containing the additional passages are distributed without dividing a PIU.

D.3.8.4 Multi-LexSum-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common legal checks in Appendix D.3, Multi-LexSum requires the question to admit a determinate procedural or legal conclusion without revealing that conclusion or the identity of the litigation collection. The candidate units must use at least three original-document excerpts, with at least two candidate units supported by each excerpt. Every candidate unit and the reference decision must pass the model-based check of source grounding. A retained problem instance must also pass the model-based solvability check with all PIUs centralized. A problem instance is rejected if it fails any of these checks.

D.3.8.5 Sensitivity to the ordering used for Pairwise PIU overlap.

The PIU-distribution conditions in Figure 4 specify which participants initially observe each PIU, but they do not prescribe an ordering based on similarity between PIUs. We therefore conduct an exploratory analysis using two additional Pairwise PIU overlap distributions for each of the 29 retained Multi-LexSum problem instances. One uses a seeded random ordering. The other uses an ordering that places PIUs with similar embedding representations next to one another.

We represent each PIU using Cohere Embed v4 (Cohere, 2025), with the clustering input type and 1,536-dimensional float embeddings, and normalize each representation. For a PIU ordering π\pi, we compute

1|ℐqmin|−1​∑j=1|ℐqmin|−1cos⁡(z⁡(iπj),z⁡(iπj+1)),\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}|-1}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}|-1}\cos\!\left(z(i_{\pi_{j}}),z(i_{\pi_{j+1}})\right),

where z⁡(⋅)z(\cdot) maps a PIU to its embedding representation. We find the ordering that maximizes this quantity using exact dynamic programming with deterministic tie breaking. The seeded comparison uses a deterministic random permutation.

For either ordering, participant j<|ℐqmin|j<|\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}| initially observes iπji_{\pi_{j}} and iπj+1i_{\pi_{j+1}}, and the final participant initially observes iπ|ℐqmin|i_{\pi_{|\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}|}}. The two distributions therefore have the same problem instance, pivotal information, number of participants, total number of PIU assignments, and number of PIUs in each participant’s initial local observation. They differ only in which PIUs occupy these positions.

We evaluate both distributions in Multi-Agent PIU-Only using Qwen3-235B-A22B, Coordinator-selected speaker, 15 participant responses, and the resource budgets used in the legal model comparison. We apply the evaluation procedure for free-form decisions in Appendix G.1.2 using GPT-5.4 as the model judge. Table 16 reports the paired results.

The maximum-similarity ordering increases the intended construction measurement: mean adjacent cosine similarity increases from .449 to .598. Its episode success rate, LLM-judged score, and answer-component coverage are descriptively higher than under the seeded random ordering. The paired difference in the LLM-judged score is 6.7 percentage points, with a problem-instance-bootstrap 95% confidence interval of [−3.1,16.3][-3.1,16.3] percentage points. Thus, this exploratory analysis does not establish a difference between the two PIU distributions. We report it to document a construction based on PIU similarity, not to rank PIU-distribution procedures or select an allocation using evaluation outcomes.

D.3.8.6 Sensitivity to the assignment of participant descriptions.

Following Step 5 of the common legal construction procedure (Appendix D.3), each participant receives a participant description constructed from the broad subject or function of its assigned PIU. The description must not disclose the PIU’s specific content, values, conclusions, or effect on the final decision. The 301 participant descriptions used across the 29 retained Multi-LexSum problem instances pass the model-based check specified in that procedure.

We construct two versions of each problem instance. In one version, each participant description is attached to the participant assigned the PIU from which the description was constructed. In the paired version, the same participant descriptions are permuted across participants. The permutation preserves every participant description, including repeated descriptions, while ensuring that the description attached to every participant changes. Apart from which participant description is attached to each participant, the paired versions have the same problem instance, pivotal information, PIU distribution, initial local observations, communication structure, and resource budgets.

We evaluate both versions in Multi-Agent PIU-Only using Qwen3-235B-A22B, Coordinator-selected speaker, 15 participant responses, and the resource budgets used in the legal model comparison. We apply the evaluation procedure for free-form decisions in Appendix G.1.2 using GPT-5.4 as the model judge. Table 17 reports the paired results.

Permuting the participant descriptions decreases the mean LLM-judged score by 30.7 percentage points. The LLM-judged score is lower after permutation for 24 problem instances, higher for three, and unchanged for two; a two-sided exact sign test gives p=4.9×10−5p=4.9\times 10^{-5}. Every PIU appears in the communication transcript in all 29 problem instances when participant descriptions are constructed from participants’ assigned PIUs, compared with 18 of 29 problem instances when the same descriptions are permuted across participants. Thus, under Coordinator-selected speaker, performance depends on whether the participant descriptions correspond to the PIUs assigned to those participants. This analysis isolates the assignment of participant descriptions; it does not compare communication structures or procedures for constructing participant descriptions.

D.3.9 SARA Problem-Instance Construction

D.3.9.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

SARA (Holzenberger et al., 2020) provides 100 tax cases with case facts, statutory text, and calculation and reasoning steps. Of these source cases, 83 yield a candidate problem instance and 63 satisfy the source and PIU requirements described below. Forty-five pass the repeated model-based solvability checks with all PIUs centralized and are retained. The retained problem instances contain 393 PIUs, with six to twelve PIUs per problem instance (mean 8.7), and four to eight answer components (mean 5.5). The legal evaluation uses all 45 retained problem instances.

D.3.9.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Construction executes the supplied calculation and reasoning steps and selects an intermediate conclusion that depends on multiple steps. The selected conclusion defines a numeric decision objective, such as a deduction, taxable income, or a tax amount, rather than requiring every problem instance to recover the original total-tax result. Construction traces the steps backward from that conclusion to the facts and rules that determine it and fixes the reference decision before writing the question.

Each candidate unit states one fact or rule needed for at least one of the selected calculation and reasoning steps. Source-stated facts and statutory rules retain their source locations. When a required relation appears only in the supplied calculation and reasoning steps, construction states that relation in ordinary legal language and records its basis. A calculated intermediate result is not repeated as a candidate unit when the supplied facts and rules already determine it. The model-based sufficiency and necessity check determines which candidate units form ℐqmin\mathcal{I}^{\min}_{q}.

The final decision must state the requested numeric result and a concise derivation. The evaluator described in Appendix G.1.2 compares the requested numeric result with the reference value and evaluates the answer components that form the derivation.

D.3.9.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

For SARA, the supplied calculation and reasoning steps are used during problem-instance construction but are not provided to participants. Each participant’s source material contains the fact or rule stated by each PIU assigned to that participant, together with the case facts and statutory text. Information stating a PIU not assigned to that participant is removed before the source material is provided.

D.3.9.4 SARA-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common legal checks in Appendix D.3, SARA requires every candidate unit to have a recorded basis in the case facts, statutory text, or supplied calculation and reasoning steps. A fact or rule must resolve each condition needed to determine the selected conclusion, including a condition that rules out an exception. We apply the PIU construction requirements in Section 3.2. Each problem instance then undergoes five model-based solvability checks with all PIUs centralized and is retained when at least four succeed. A problem instance is rejected if it fails any of these checks.

D.4 Finance

We construct finance problem instances from FinDVer (Zhao et al., 2024) and FinLongDocQA (Wang et al., 2026). Each source corpus corresponds to one problem family, which we call the FinDVer and FinLongDocQA problem families, respectively. The procedure below reports the choices specific to these source corpora and problem families. Table 18 summarizes the finance problem families and their source corpora.

D.4.1 Common Finance Construction Procedure

D.4.1.1 Step 1. Select the underlying source materials.

A problem instance uses exactly one U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing or company-year annual report. Native questions, answers, labels, source-text references, and available calculations, code, and reasoning may be used during construction but do not form part of the initial common observation.

D.4.1.2 Step 2. Divide the underlying source materials.

The filing or report is divided into complete paragraphs and tables while preserving their source locations. Adjacent fragments may be combined only when a label in one fragment requires a value in the other to be complete. A table is not divided into individual cells or values.

D.4.1.3 Step 3. Identify candidate units.

For each source question, a model-based source-grounding check identifies every paragraph, table, or combination of an adjacent label and value that contributes a report-specific value, definition, period, unit, entity scope, condition, exception, or contradiction needed to reconstruct the source annotation. Before problem-instance construction, the procedure records whether candidate units are exact duplicates, whether one fully contains another, whether one can be derived from another, and whether they partially overlap. A candidate unit is removed only when a retained candidate unit contains its entire contribution; partial overlap alone does not support removal.

D.4.1.4 Step 4. Specify the decision objective and format.

Construction combines one or more source questions and at least two candidate units into a problem instance with a free-form decision format. It fixes the reference decision, answer components, the candidate units supporting each answer component, and the evaluation criteria for values, units, periods, signs, scopes, and conclusions.

D.4.1.5 Step 5. Identify the pivotal information.

Each candidate unit is one paragraph, complete table, or combined adjacent label and value. We apply the PIU construction and removal checks in Section 3.2, using the answer components to assess completeness, correctness, and source grounding. A redundant candidate unit is removed before the checks are repeated.

D.4.1.6 Step 6. Construct participant descriptions.

Each participant receives a source-corpus-specific reviewer description. These descriptions identify the participant as a reviewer of a filing or annual report and include a participant number. Construction records broad information features for PIUs, but participant descriptions and the participant directory do not disclose PIU values, calculations, conclusions, or their effect on the reference decision.

D.4.1.7 Step 7. Define the PIU distribution and distribute source material.

Each finance problem instance uses the One PIU per participant condition in the two team evaluation conditions. The additional PIU distributions reported in Table 19 use the other conditions from Figure 4. After each PIU distribution is fixed, the underlying source materials are distributed across participants. The source material provided to each participant is checked for information that contains or supports reconstruction of a PIU assigned to another participant. Such material is removed while every PIU assigned to that participant is retained.

This source-material check concerns meaning rather than exact wording. Exact repetition of a PIU assigned to another participant is sufficient for removal but is not required: a passage or collection of passages is also removed when it supports reconstruction of the report-specific value, period, unit, entity scope, condition, exception, or conclusion contributed by that PIU. Partial topical overlap alone does not support removal. After revising the source material, the procedure repeats the participant-level check while preserving every PIU assigned to that participant.

D.4.1.8 Step 8. Complete problem-instance construction.

A problem instance is retained only after the specified participants, pivotal information, PIU distribution, reference decision, and distributed source material pass the applicable checks.

D.4.2 Problem Instances and PIU Distributions in the Finance Evaluation

The construction pipeline produces 389 FinDVer problem instances and 249 FinLongDocQA problem instances. Following the same fixed-subset convention used for CUAD and MAUD, the finance evaluation uses 30 problem instances from each source corpus under the three evaluation conditions. The FinDVer subset is selected deterministically in released order within source-material strata, with 20 Form 10-K filings and 10 Form 10-Q filings. The FinLongDocQA subset is selected deterministically in released order within year strata, with 9 reports from 2022, 10 from 2023, and 11 from 2024. For each language-model policy, these conditions contain 90 FinDVer episodes and 90 FinLongDocQA episodes. Each problem instance uses the One PIU per participant condition in the two team conditions.

We also construct PIU distributions under the other conditions in Figure 4. For each distribution, the initial local observation of each participant is checked for information that contains or supports reconstruction of a PIU assigned to another participant. Table 19 reports the number of evaluated problem instances admitting each PIU-distribution condition.

D.4.3 Finance Problem-Instance and PIU-Distribution Statistics

D.4.3.1 Source-corpus and problem-instance counts.

Each problem instance uses underlying source materials from one filing or company-year report. Underlying source materials from different filings or reports are not combined. Table 20 separates the available source-material pools from the processed and retained construction outputs.

The finance evaluation uses a fixed subset of 30 constructed problem instances from each source corpus, as described in Appendix D.4.2.

D.4.3.2 Problem-instance and PIU-distribution statistics.

Each problem instance requires a source-grounded written final decision. Source questions are used only during construction; the constructed question does not provide the corpus-provided answer or its label, explanation, or calculation. It also omits the PIU identity and hidden evaluation annotations. The fixed FinDVer evaluation set records 231 answer components across 70 source questions and uses 20 Form 10-K filings and 10 Form 10-Q filings. The fixed FinLongDocQA evaluation set records 64 answer components across 63 source questions and uses 9 company-year reports from 2022, 10 from 2023, and 11 from 2024. Across all 60 evaluated problem instances, every referenced source-material unit and PIU has a recorded source location, and no participant initially receives every PIU.

Figure 9 reports the PIU count and PIU length for the 60 problem instances in the finance evaluation. It also reports participant count and the length of source material provided to participants for the 277 PIU distributions under the five PIU-distribution conditions in Figure 4. For the PIU-count and PIU-length panels, each point is one problem instance; for the participant-count and source-material-length panels, each point is one PIU distribution.

Source-material length sums the material provided to each participant. Repeated material is counted for each participant who receives it because it contributes separately to that participant’s initial local observation. The source-material lengths are measured after the participant-level leakage-removal step and after applying the 40,000-token initial-local-observation cap. PIU length is measured from the PIU text supplied in Multi-Agent PIU-Only. All lengths use the same cl100k_base tokenizer used for the legal statistics.

D.4.3.3 Evaluation criteria.

In both finance source corpora, a PIU may support several answer components, and one answer component may require several PIUs. Written final decisions are graded using problem-specific criteria for values, units, periods, signs, scopes, calculations, and qualifying conclusions.

D.4.4 FinDVer Problem-Instance Construction

D.4.4.1 Source corpus and constructed problem instances.

FinDVer provides entailment, numeric, and knowledge-oriented source questions linked to SEC filings. Construction uses the FinDVer source corpus’s testmini split and retains the source location for each Form 10-K or Form 10-Q filing. The procedure constructs 389 problem instances. The finance evaluation uses the fixed 30-instance subset described in Appendix D.4.2.

D.4.4.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Construction does not use the original FinDVer question as the decision objective. Instead, it constructs a free-response filing-review task that asks for related filing-specific findings, calculations, comparisons, or classifications without providing the source values or expected conclusions. The reference decision is a source-grounded written final decision. Hidden evaluation annotations record the answer components, the links between answer components and PIUs, and problem-specific evaluation criteria. For numeric answer components, the criteria record the value, unit, sign, period, and tolerance. For textual and classification answer components, the criteria record the accepted conclusion and required scope.

Construction reconstructs each source annotation from complete filing paragraphs or tables and records overlap, containment, and derived equivalence among the candidate units before forming one filing-review problem instance. The task-generation step selects complete candidate units. It prefers a broad coherent cluster when distinct candidate units concern the same company, period, transaction, segment, liquidity topic, accounting policy, operating trend, or filing-review objective. Candidate units concerning unrelated information are excluded, and a candidate unit may be retained with another partially overlapping unit only when the task and evaluation criteria use a distinct contribution from each. Every PIU must be needed for at least one answer component, and every selected PIU is linked to the component or reasoning step it supports.

D.4.4.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

Complete filing material is distributed across participants. Surrounding passages or tables that directly repeat, tabulate, or clearly paraphrase a PIU assigned to another participant are removed. BM25 lexical scores provide candidate pointers for review, after which a model-based check inspects the complete packet and determines whether any context contains or supports reconstruction of such a PIU. The procedure performs one removal pass without redistributing the remaining source material. Every assigned PIU remains in the corresponding participant’s initial local observation.

D.4.4.4 Participant descriptions.

Participant descriptions are finance-specific reviewer labels. They may describe a broad filing or report topic, but they do not disclose PIU values, calculations, conclusions, or their effect on the reference decision.

D.4.4.5 FinDVer-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common finance checks in Appendix D.4.1, a model-based source-grounding check verifies the calculations, comparisons, scopes, and links between PIUs and answer components. Additional checks require the pivotal information to support a complete and correct final decision, require public information without PIUs to be insufficient, and reject candidate PIUs that are redundant under the answer-component links. A problem instance is rejected if it fails these checks or the common finance checks.

D.4.5 FinLongDocQA Problem-Instance Construction

D.4.5.1 Source corpus and constructed problem instances.

Each FinLongDocQA source question provides its answer type and annotated page numbers. Its reasoning and code are not used in construction. The procedure constructs 249 problem instances. The finance evaluation uses the fixed 30-instance subset described in Appendix D.4.2.

D.4.5.2 Decision objective and PIU construction.

Construction does not use a source question verbatim as the decision objective. It constructs a free-response annual-report task that asks for a written memo, calculation, explanation, or numbered review. The task may use one source question or combine several source questions from the same company-year report. When the selected source questions do not share one analytical purpose, construction asks a concise multi-part review rather than inventing a causal relationship or comparison. It records a reference decision, answer components, links between PIUs and answer components, evaluation criteria, and errors that make a final decision incorrect. Written final decisions are evaluated using the recorded problem-specific evaluation criteria.

For each source question, construction uses the annotated pages to identify every paragraph, table, or combined adjacent label and value needed for the answer’s values, definitions, periods, units, scope, and exceptions. These candidate units then follow the division and overlap requirements in Appendix D.4.1. Each selected evidence unit is one complete mapped block. A block is not duplicated into multiple PIUs for separate values, rows, or claims. Every selected PIU must support at least one report-specific claim, and removing that PIU must leave at least one linked claim not fully grounded even when all other PIUs remain available. A PIU may support several claims, and one claim may require several PIUs.

D.4.5.3 Source material and PIU distribution.

Each PIU is provided to the participant assigned that PIU. Other report passages and tables are provided to the participant with the shortest initial local observation, using distance from the page containing that participant’s PIU to resolve a tie. A model-based check determines whether one passage or table, or several in combination, supports reconstruction of a PIU assigned to another participant. The source material is revised until every PIU is preserved and such information is removed.

When unrelated rows of a large table independently state a PIU assigned to another participant, the table is restricted to the rows supporting the answer component associated with the PIU assigned to that participant.

D.4.5.4 Participant descriptions.

Participant descriptions are finance-specific reviewer labels. They may describe a broad filing or report topic, such as liquidity and capital resources or deferred tax assets and liabilities, but they do not disclose PIU values, calculations, conclusions, or their effect on the reference decision.

D.4.5.5 FinLongDocQA-specific construction checks.

In addition to the common finance checks in Appendix D.4.1, a problem instance is rejected if a participant does not receive a PIU assigned to that participant or if source material still supports reconstruction of a PIU assigned to another participant. Additional checks require the reference answer to satisfy every recorded claim, preserve material units and periods, and use no outside facts. A problem instance is rejected if it fails these checks or the common finance checks.

D.5 Medical

We construct medical problem instances from MLCR (Wisedocs, 2026) and EvidenceBench (Wang et al., 2025). Each source corpus corresponds to one problem family: MLCR medical-record reasoning and EvidenceBench biomedical-evidence reasoning. The procedure below reports the choices specific to these source corpora and problem families. Table 22 summarizes the medical problem families and their source corpora.

D.5.1 Common Medical Construction Procedure

D.5.1.1 Step 1. Select the underlying source materials.

A problem instance uses source materials from one medical source record. For EvidenceBench, this is one biomedical paper represented as an ordered sentence pool. For MLCR, this is one case whose source material may contain many visit summary documents. Source materials from different papers or cases are not combined.

D.5.1.2 Step 2. Divide the underlying source materials.

EvidenceBench source materials are divided into paper sentences, preserving sentence indices and sentence types. MLCR source materials are divided into exact sentence-like atoms and paragraph spans with raw character offsets, document identifiers, and checksums. Adjacent atoms or sentences may be combined only when needed to preserve a patient, date, encounter, negation, measurement unit, uncertainty, abbreviation, comparison, or clinical scope.

D.5.1.3 Step 3. Identify candidate units.

Construction uses source annotations to identify candidate evidence units. EvidenceBench starts from annotated optimal-evidence anchors. MLCR first maps source question-answer pairs to exact source atoms in the case record. In both families, candidate units are source-faithful evidence spans rather than final PIUs: they become PIUs only after task construction and the boundary checks show that they are answer-relevant and necessary.

D.5.1.4 Step 4. Specify the decision objective and format.

Construction creates a free-response medical task with a written reference decision and a hidden claim-level rubric. The public task does not reveal PIU identities, candidate-unit identifiers, source annotation labels, hidden rubric claims, reference decisions, or expected values and conclusions. Required claims record medical scope, patient or study population, dates or periods, comparisons, outcomes, direction, uncertainty, units, tolerances, and causal or associational strength when applicable.

D.5.1.5 Step 5. Identify the pivotal information.

We apply the PIU construction requirements in Section 3.2. The pivotal information must support a complete and grounded answer to the public task, while a missing PIU must leave at least one required claim unsupported or incorrect. A model-based solver and separate judge check the all-PIU condition, a no-PIU condition, and leave-one-out conditions. The solver sees only the public task and displayed source material; the judge uses the hidden rubric to evaluate claim correctness and grounding. Correct guesses that are not grounded in displayed material do not satisfy the grounding check.

D.5.1.6 Step 6. Define the PIU distribution and distribute source material.

Each medical problem instance uses the One PIU per participant condition in the two team evaluation conditions. The additional PIU distributions reported in Table 23 use the other conditions from Figure 4. After each PIU distribution is fixed, source material is distributed across participants. The material provided to each participant is checked for information that contains or supports reconstruction of a PIU assigned to another participant. Such material is removed while every PIU assigned to that participant is retained.

D.5.1.7 Step 7. Complete problem-instance construction.

A problem instance is retained only after the public task, pivotal information, PIU distribution, reference decision, hidden rubric, and distributed source material pass the applicable checks.

D.5.2 Problem Instances and PIU Distributions in the Medical Evaluation

The final medical evaluation uses 29 MLCR problem instances and 45 EvidenceBench problem instances under the three evaluation conditions. For each language-model policy, these conditions contain 87 MLCR episodes and 135 EvidenceBench episodes.

We also construct PIU distributions under the other conditions in Figure 4. For each distribution, the initial local observation of each participant is checked for information that contains or supports reconstruction of a PIU assigned to another participant. Table 23 reports the number of evaluated problem instances admitting each PIU-distribution condition.

D.5.3 Medical Problem-Instance and PIU-Distribution Statistics

D.5.3.1 Source-corpus and problem-instance counts.

Each problem instance uses one EvidenceBench paper or one MLCR case. For MLCR, the case may contain many underlying visit-summary source documents, but cases are not combined. Table 24 separates the available source-material pools from the fixed evaluation problem instances.

D.5.3.2 Problem-instance and PIU-distribution statistics.

Each medical problem instance requires a source-grounded written final decision. The constructed public question omits the source-provided answer, expected conclusion, PIU identities, and hidden claim rubric. Across the 74 evaluated problem instances, every PIU has a source location, and no participant initially receives every PIU in the team evaluation conditions.

Figure 10 reports the PIU count and PIU length for the 74 problem instances in the final medical evaluation. It also reports participant count and the length of source material provided to participants for the 321 PIU distributions under the five PIU-distribution conditions in Figure 4. For the PIU-count and PIU-length panels, each point is one problem instance; for the participant-count and source-material-length panels, each point is one PIU distribution.

Source-material length sums the material provided to each participant. Repeated material is counted for each participant who receives it because it contributes separately to that participant’s initial local observation. The source-material lengths are measured after the participant-level leakage-removal step and after applying the 40,000-token initial-local-observation cap. PIU length is measured from the PIU text supplied in Multi-Agent PIU-Only. All lengths use the same cl100k_base tokenizer used for the legal statistics.

D.5.3.3 Evaluation criteria.

In both medical source corpora, a PIU may support several required claims, and one required claim may require several PIUs. Written final decisions are graded using problem-specific criteria for clinical scope, study or patient population, dates or periods, measurements, units, direction, uncertainty, comparison, and causal or associational strength.

D.5.4 MLCR Problem-Instance Construction

D.5.4.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

MLCR provides long medical-record cases with source questions, reference answers, and visit-summary source documents (Wisedocs, 2026). The evaluated construction uses 29 problem instances. Because an MLCR case may contain many visit summaries, a single problem instance can draw source material from multiple source documents within the same case, but it never combines source material across cases.

D.5.4.2 Decision objective, reference decision, and evaluation criteria.

Construction first maps each eligible source question-answer pair to exact source atoms that materially reconstruct the answer. It then groups one or more source question-answer pairs from the same case into a clinically coherent free-response task. When selected source questions do not share one clinical or claims-review purpose, construction uses a concise multi-part review rather than inventing a causal relationship or common theme. The public task asks for the medical-record review and does not reveal source question identifiers, candidate identifiers, PIU identifiers, or case-specific expected values and conclusions.

The hidden rubric records required claims, the selected evidence units that support each claim, and the criteria for clinical scope, dates, encounters, measurements, units, direction, negation, uncertainty, and causal strength. The reference decision must satisfy all required claims using only the selected source evidence. Generic medical knowledge may connect observations but cannot replace missing patient-specific evidence.

D.5.4.3 Candidate-unit and PIU construction.

MLCR source documents are divided into exact source atoms while preserving raw offsets and document identifiers. Each candidate unit is a contiguous span of atoms from one source document. Adjacent atoms are included only when needed to preserve patient, date, encounter, negation, measurement unit, uncertainty, or clinical scope. Non-adjacent evidence and repeated equivalents are kept separate rather than merged.

A model-based grounding check verifies that every required claim and every material statement in the reference decision are grounded in the selected exact source evidence, and that each selected unit makes a unique necessary contribution. Boundary checks then test the complete selected set, a no-PIU condition, and leave-one-out conditions. A selected candidate becomes a PIU only after these checks show that the full set is sufficient and that removing the candidate breaks at least one claim it supports.

D.5.4.4 Source material and PIU distribution.

MLCR source material is distributed across participants under the PIU distribution. The participant assigned a PIU receives the canonical source span for that PIU. Additional source atoms from the same case are assigned to participants subject to the 40,000-token local-observation budget. Multi-Agent PIU-Only presents only the assigned PIU text. Multi-Agent Full-Context presents the participant’s medical-record source material with neutral source-file structure. Single-Agent All-PIU presents all pivotal information. All three conditions use the same public task, and hidden source mappings, candidate identifiers, PIU identifiers, rubric mappings, and reference answers are not shown to decision makers.

D.5.4.5 MLCR-specific construction checks.

For each participant and each PIU assigned to another participant, a model-based packet-leakage check determines whether the participant’s complete full-context packet directly contains, duplicates, paraphrases, or permits reconstruction of that foreign PIU, including by combining multiple packet passages. Source material containing the participant’s assigned PIU is not removed. If noncanonical source material reconstructs a foreign PIU, removable contexts are deleted and the packet is checked again. If the participant’s own canonical source span itself reveals a foreign PIU, construction records this as canonical overlap and either merges ownership as allowed by the admissible allocation or rejects the allocation when strict one-each ownership is required. A problem instance or allocation is rejected if leakage remains without removable source material or the check does not converge.

D.5.5 EvidenceBench Problem-Instance Construction

D.5.5.1 Source corpus and retained problem instances.

EvidenceBench provides biomedical hypotheses, full papers represented as ordered sentence pools, sentence types, and sentence-level annotations of the minimum evidence required for each hypothesis (Wang et al., 2025). We use the test split. Forty-five problem instances pass the construction checks, and all 45 are used in the medical evaluation.

We treat the sentences identified by these annotations as source locations used during construction rather than as PIUs. For every source record, construction records the instance and paper identifiers, original hypothesis, ordered sentence indices, sentence types, paper-sentence count, split, and source-file hash as hidden source annotations. Up to two neighboring sentences may be added only to restore an incomplete referent, comparison, abbreviation, or measurement context; the complete neighborhood is not automatically included in a candidate unit.

D.5.5.2 Decision objective, reference decision, and evaluation criteria.

Construction turns the source hypothesis and grounded evidence annotations into a biomedical question, a reference decision, and separately evaluated answer components. The decision objective omits the annotated sentence indices, PIU identities, candidate-unit identifiers, reference decision, and hidden construction information. The hypothesis guides the question but is not necessarily reused verbatim: the question may instead ask for the population, exposure or intervention, comparator, outcome, direction, evidentiary strength, or required limitation established by the paper evidence. The reference decision uses only selected exact evidence and preserves medical scope and the source’s causal or associational strength.

Answer components and candidate units are distinct. An answer component may require several candidate units that make complementary contributions, and one candidate unit may support several answer components. The hidden evaluation criteria therefore record the links between answer components and candidate units. For some answer components, every linked candidate unit is required; for others, any one of several linked candidate units is sufficient. The recorded links state which part of an answer component each candidate unit supports. Construction also records, for every candidate unit, whether it is retained and, if it is excluded, the reason for exclusion.

D.5.5.3 Candidate-unit construction and checks.

Construction preserves a one-to-one relation between the sentences identified by the source annotations and candidate units. Each such sentence produces exactly one candidate unit, and distinct source sentences are not merged even when they jointly support the same answer component. The candidate unit contains the source sentence verbatim and may add only the minimal contiguous neighboring context needed to make it interpretable. It may not include another sentence identified by the source annotations as context. Construction checks complete one-to-one coverage of the source annotations, unique identifiers, contiguous and nonoverlapping sentence spans, exact agreement with the paper text, and absence of another sentence identified by the source annotations. Relations among candidate units are represented by their links to answer components rather than by merging their source locations.

A separate model-based check receives the decision objective, reference decision, hidden evaluation criteria, and the complete candidate-unit set, including excluded candidate units. For each retained candidate unit, it checks relevance to the decision objective, direct support, and necessity under the recorded links to answer components; for each excluded candidate unit, it checks that exclusion is justified. It also checks that the decision objective is natural rather than artificially expanded to accommodate unrelated evidence, that every answer component and the reference decision are source-grounded, and that population, comparison, outcome, direction, uncertainty, and causal scope are preserved. A failed check permits bounded revision of the decision objective, answer components, and links while the exact candidate units remain fixed. At least two annotated source sentences and two retained candidate units are required, but construction imposes no fixed upper bound.

D.5.5.4 PIU construction and checks.

Construction then applies the model-based removal check described in Section 3.2, using a model and a separate model judge. The model receives only the decision objective, the paper excerpts available in the current check, and neutral evidence numbers. It does not receive candidate-unit, PIU, annotated-sentence, answer-component, or omitted-unit identifiers. The model judge receives the hidden evaluation criteria and reference decision and separately records whether each answer component is correct and grounded in the material provided to the model. A correct guess is not treated as grounded.

With all retained candidate units, every answer component must be correct and grounded, the final decision must be complete, and it must contain no critical error. For each removal required by Section 3.2, at least one answer component linked to the removed candidate unit must cease to be satisfied. The recorded links are also checked against the source references in the model’s response: every linked unit is required when the answer component requires all of them, whereas at least one linked unit is required when any one is sufficient. After every check passes, each retained candidate unit forms one PIU; candidate units that jointly support one answer component remain separate PIUs.

D.5.5.5 Source material and PIU distribution.

The retained construction uses One PIU per participant. Each source sentence containing a PIU is reserved for the participant assigned that PIU. Overlap between the source sentences containing distinct PIUs is rejected. Every remaining sentence from the EvidenceBench paper sentence pool is then assigned to exactly one participant, with seeded assignment balancing the estimated lengths of the initial local observations; the resulting division is exhaustive and disjoint. Multi-Agent PIU-Only presents only the exact text of the assigned PIU. Multi-Agent Full-Context presents the participant’s paper sentences with neutral source identifiers. Single-Agent All-PIU presents all pivotal information. All three conditions use the same decision objective, and hidden candidate-unit identifiers, PIU identifiers, annotated source locations, links to answer components, reference source locations, and source-material check information are removed from the decision makers’ observations.

D.5.5.6 EvidenceBench-specific construction checks.

For each participant and each PIU assigned to another participant, a model-based check considers the participant’s complete initial local observation rather than isolated lexical matches. The initial local observation contains a PIU assigned to another participant only when an exact duplicate, clear paraphrase, equivalent reported result, or combination of source passages supports that PIU’s complete contribution at the same medical scope. Shared topics, partial overlap in population or outcome, a different measurement, a general mechanistic association, or a plausible inference requiring external knowledge do not suffice.

When such reconstruction is possible, the removable additional source passages that support the reconstruction are deleted, and every participant and PIU assigned to another participant are checked again. Source material containing the participant’s assigned PIU is never deleted. If that material alone supports a PIU assigned to another participant, the problem instance is rejected because a candidate unit is incorrectly defined. The procedure permits at most three revisions and rejects the problem instance if the initial local observation still contains another participant’s PIU, no removable source material exists, final-decision validation fails, or the checks do not converge.

D.6 Software Engineering

We construct software-engineering problem instances from SWE Atlas Codebase QnA (Raghavendra et al., 2026) and DeepSWE (Huang et al., 2026). Table 26 summarizes the source corpora, problem families, evaluation criteria, and evaluation scope. The two source corpora use separate construction procedures, described in the following subsections.

D.6.1 Source Corpora and Evaluation Scope

D.6.1.1 Shared construction conventions.

Both source corpora fix a repository and base commit, identify exact source-grounded PIUs, assign each PIU to one participant in collaborative conditions, and withhold reference answers and hidden qualification records from the evaluated agents. Source-specific procedures determine how code, tests, runtime observations, and additional context are collected, grouped, distributed, and checked for leakage and format salience.

The SWE Atlas evaluation uses all 32 retained instances and eight language-model policies across the three evaluation conditions. For DeepSWE, we archive intermediate construction and allocation artifacts for 21 screened candidate tasks, then complete construction for a frozen 12-task cohort selected to preserve programming-language coverage and variation in original benchmark difficulty. These 12 tasks constitute both the constructed and evaluated DeepSWE problem instances reported in Table 2. The source-specific construction and evaluation procedures are described below.

D.6.2 Software-Engineering Problem-Instance Statistics

Figure 11 and Table 27 report structural statistics for both software-engineering source corpora. For SWE Atlas, the problem-instance measures use the 32 one-each instances, while distribution measures use the 157 valid distributions across the five allocation modes. For DeepSWE, both sets of measures use the fixed 12-task evaluation cohort and its functional one-each allocations. Tasks outside this fixed cohort are not included in these descriptive statistics.

The code/source-unit column counts Atlas context units and DeepSWE code fragments. The runtime-observation column counts explicitly recorded execution observations. PIU length is measured from the evidence assigned to each PIU. Full source-material length uses the underlying Atlas source units or the DeepSWE code archive, observations, and public-check catalog. The distribution column reports assigned participant packets; for DeepSWE these are the available PIU evidence packets before finalized full-context distractor packing. All lengths use the cl100k_base tokenizer.

D.6.3 SWE Atlas Codebase QnA Problem-Instance Construction

D.6.3.1 Source corpus and decision objective.

SWE Atlas Codebase QnA asks for a source-grounded technical decision about a repository fixed at a recorded base commit. Construction loads the task question, positive and negative evaluation criteria, corpus-provided answer, Docker image, and base commit. The reference decision and evaluation criteria are used for hidden construction checks but are not shown to the agents that search the repository or receive the released evidence. Thirty-two of the 124 official entries pass the completed construction procedure and are retained.

D.6.3.2 Evidence collection and candidate units.

Construction collects exact source, test, configuration, documentation, and, when a criterion requires observed behavior, runtime evidence from the unchanged Docker checkout. Runtime commands use the installed repository tools, do not use the network or install packages, and record their output, exit status, commit, and repository state. A runtime observation is included only with the source or test evidence needed to interpret it; runtime output alone does not form a PIU.

Candidate units are exact contiguous source-material spans that establish one answer contribution. Source, test, and runtime spans are grouped when they jointly establish one indivisible proposition; duplicates and fully contained contributions are merged, while independent contributions remain separate. Navigation results and model-written summaries are excluded. The construction does not target a fixed PIU count and retains at least two PIUs per collaborative problem instance.

D.6.3.3 Grounding, sufficiency, and necessity checks.

Construction evaluates the complete candidate set, the decision objective with no candidate units, and each leave-one-out removal. The solver receives only the exact evidence available in the current check, while a separate judge assesses correctness and source grounding. A candidate is retained only when the complete set supports every required positive and negative criterion, the no-unit condition fails, and removing that candidate causes the linked answer component to fail. Candidate grouping or evidence collection is revised and the checks are repeated when these conditions do not hold.

D.6.3.4 PIU distribution and evaluation conditions.

The evaluated distribution uses One PIU per participant. Source or test units and runtime output containing a PIU are reserved for its owner; additional context is assigned without duplication unless the allocation condition explicitly permits overlap. Multi-Agent PIU-Only provides the assigned PIU evidence, Multi-Agent Full-Context adds neutral additional repository material and actual runtime output, and Single-Agent All-PIU provides all pivotal information in a fixed order. The common observation identifies the task, repository, base commit, and response format without exposing PIU ownership or reference answers.

D.6.3.5 Atlas-specific leakage and salience checks.

For every participant, a model-based check determines whether the initial local observation contains or supports a PIU assigned to another participant, including information reconstructable by combining multiple passages. Topical overlap alone does not count. Revisions may remove or reassign additional context but may not remove the owner’s PIU evidence. The procedure also checks that PIU-bearing material is not identifiable from position, wrapper, annotation, or conspicuous length, and excludes instances that still contain foreign PIU information after bounded revision.

D.6.4 DeepSWE Problem-Instance Construction

DeepSWE provides long-horizon repository-level code-repair tasks, each defined by a pinned base repository, a public task instruction, and an official hidden verifier. A task may admit multiple verifier-passing patches, and repeated attempts by the same model may follow different search and implementation paths. The original DeepSWE evaluation accounts for this variation through repeated rollouts: its analysis uses three independent attempts by the same model on each task, while its final evaluation uses approximately four rollouts per task and model configuration. Successful GPT-5.5 repair trajectories take roughly 80 agent steps on average (Huang et al., 2026).

Our goal is not to reproduce this unrestricted long-horizon search, but to control the evidence required for collaboration under a fixed execution budget. We therefore define a DeepSWE PIU as a unit of functional evidence needed to support a successful repair under a fixed, bounded protocol. The complete PIU set is constructed so that, together with the public task instruction, it supports a verifier-passing patch using a restricted action space and five atomic edit turns.

D.6.4.1 Instruction-only screening.

We begin with 40 DeepSWE tasks. For each task, the model receives the public task instruction but no PIUs or additional code evidence. We give the model the same five-turn repair budget used in the subsequent evidence-bundle checks and run three independent attempts. We continue PIU construction only for tasks that fail all three instruction-only attempts. This screen removes tasks whose instructions already provide enough information to locate and implement a repair within the bounded protocol. The instruction-only runs therefore serve as the no-evidence, or “none,” condition for construction.

D.6.4.2 Constructor-only materials and evidence collection.

For each candidate task, the constructor may inspect the reference patch, hidden-test patch and identifiers, public-check definitions and results, and the pinned base repository to locate implementation boundaries and audit evidence coverage. These materials are construction-only: the reference patch, hidden tests, verifier internals, hidden expected values, and constructor rationales are never copied into solver-visible evidence or exposed to evaluated agents. The public task instruction is common input to every condition and is not itself a PIU.

Construction collects exact task-relevant fragments from the unmodified base commit and deterministic runtime observations produced from the same checkout. Each observation records the executed probe, its output and exit status, and the repository state needed to interpret it. Observations may describe public base-repository behavior but do not reveal hidden assertions, hidden expected values, or solution code. Solver-visible evidence is therefore composed of base-commit code and reproducible base-repository behavior, not pieces of the reference patch.

D.6.4.3 Functional PIU construction.

A DeepSWE task may admit multiple implementations that pass the official verifier. Searching for a minimal evidence set relative to one reference patch could therefore steer the agent toward only one implementation path despite the existence of other valid repairs. We instead define each DeepSWE PIU to represent one coherent functional behavior or contract required by the verifier, rather than a fragment of a particular reference implementation.

A functional PIU may combine several exact code fragments with deterministic runtime observations when they jointly specify an implementation boundary, such as parsing and validation, state accumulation, lifecycle and cleanup, persistence, public-API wiring, or error propagation. Supporting types, callers, interfaces, and exports are included when they are required to implement that behavior. Each selected code fragment or observation is assigned to exactly one PIU. Functional labels, evidence-selection rationales, and hidden failure information remain constructor metadata and are not included in participant packets.

The purpose of these PIUs is not to reproduce the reference patch. Each PIU is grounded in base-repository code and reproducible runtime behavior, and the complete PIU set must support a verifier-passing repair under the bounded protocol.

D.6.4.4 Bounded evidence-bundle checks.

We inspect candidate PIU bundles with the same source-restricted repair interface used in evaluation. The patch author has five atomic edit turns and may invoke checks from a frozen public-check catalog. Repository mutation is restricted to replace, write, and delete operations, and the agent may terminate before using all five turns. After termination, the official hidden verifier is run once. Success is determined solely by whether the final patch passes this verifier; matching the reference patch is not required.

Each complete PIU bundle is evaluated in three independent qualification runs. These runs form the complete-evidence, or “all,” condition for construction. When all three instruction-only runs fail but the complete bundle enables a successful repair within the same five-turn protocol, the bundle provides operational evidence of sufficiency under that bounded protocol.

Repeated qualification outcomes and targeted leave-one-PIU-out checks are used diagnostically to refine the evidence bundle. We inspect whether removing a PIU reduces repair success or removes a functional boundary needed for the repair, and use the result to identify missing, irrelevant, or redundant evidence. Because repair trajectories are stochastic and multiple patches may pass the verifier, these leave-one-out checks are not treated as a formal proof of necessity over every possible repair procedure. They diagnose the contribution of each functional PIU under the fixed five-turn protocol.

D.6.4.5 Final evaluation cohort.

After screening, evidence-bundle construction, and qualification, we freeze a 12-task evaluation cohort from the initial 40 tasks. The cohort contains four Go, four Python, two JavaScript, and two TypeScript tasks and preserves both programming-language coverage and variation in original benchmark difficulty. These 12 tasks are the constructed and evaluated DeepSWE problem instances reported in Table 2.

D.6.4.6 PIU allocation and evaluation conditions.

The final functional PIUs are assigned one per participant. In Single-Agent All-PIU, one patch author receives the ordered union of all PIU evidence. In Multi-Agent PIU-Only, each participant receives only its assigned functional PIU. In Multi-Agent Full-Context, each participant receives its assigned PIU together with non-PIU base-repository code and additional runtime context.

Non-PIU code fragments in the Full-Context packets are distributed exclusively across participants. Additional runtime context uses only previously collected observations; selected non-owned observations may be duplicated as distractors across participant packets. No participant receives the entire repository. The collaborative transcript is sequential and coordinator-selected, and the final patch author acts on the public transcript using the same five-turn repair interface and public-check catalog. No condition exposes PIU identifiers, the reference patch, hidden-test information, hidden expected values, or constructor rationales.

D.6.4.7 Repeated-run aggregation and failure handling.

To account for stochastic repair trajectories, we schedule three independent runs for each task–model–condition combination. Within each task and condition, we first average the available verifier outcomes across repetitions and then average across the 12 tasks, giving each task equal weight.

A completed verifier failure, an ordinary unsuccessful repair, or a confirmed context-window failure receives a score of zero and remains in the denominator. A run is marked unavailable and excluded only when no valid task outcome can be obtained because of provider-capacity, API or serving, container or Docker, or missing-verifier-result failures. Availability exclusions are recorded separately from completed task failures.

D.7 Independent Validation of PIU Construction

All problem instances undergo checks during PIU construction, and the participant-level source-material check is performed after source-material distribution. Centralized solver success additionally establishes operational answerability, but does not by itself validate leave-one-out pivotality or the participant-level source-material check. We therefore conducted an additional post-construction audit of 20 instances from the fixed 30-instance MAUD evaluation set and 20 instances from the fixed 30-instance FinLongDocQA evaluation set. We used GPT-5.4, which was not used for instance construction, as the primary evaluator. The sample was frozen before evaluation. The audit covered every selected instance under every PIU leave-one-out removal and each participant’s initial local observation together with the initial common observation. Solver outputs and answer accuracy were not used as evidence in these judgments.

For the leave-one-out pivotality check, a removal passes only when the linked answer component becomes unsupported or genuinely unresolved. The participant-level source-material check passes at the instance level only when no participant’s initial local observation together with the initial common observation grounds the complete reference decision.

Across the two validated construction regimes, the leave-one-out results provide the strongest evidence that retained PIUs are individually pivotal. The participant-level source-material check finds that no participant’s initial observation is sufficient for a complete grounded decision in any selected FinLongDocQA instance and identifies two MAUD instances in which one participant’s initial observation together with the initial common observation is sufficient.

Appendix E Evaluation Results Across Domains and Source Corpora

The first three subsections disaggregate the model–domain results in Figure 6. Every reported comparison uses the same problem instances, their pivotal information, and the problem-specific evaluator across the three evaluation conditions within a source corpus. The legal, finance, medical, and software-engineering evaluations use One PIU per participant. All team episodes use Coordinator-selected speaker with 15 participant responses before the final decision. Within each model–source-corpus comparison, the two multi-agent conditions hold this PIU distribution, communication structure, and the source-corpus-specific resource budgets fixed. The results do not pool different communication structures or PIU-distribution conditions within an episode. For the three evaluation conditions in Figure 6, confirmed context-window failures count as unsuccessful episodes, whereas episodes without a valid outcome because of provider-capacity or other infrastructure failures are unavailable.

E.1 Source-Corpus Results

Table 29 reports episode success rate for each source corpus and gives equal weight to the models. The model–domain results in Figure 6 pool problem instances across the source corpora within each model.

E.2 Model and Source-Corpus Results

Table 30 reports the complete three-condition model and source-corpus results underlying the domain and source-corpus summaries, together with available Single-Agent Full-Context estimates. In that condition, one model receives the ordered union of the source material assigned under the same fixed PIU distribution. Each row averages episode success over the fixed problem instances for one model and source corpus. Within a row, the two multi-agent conditions use the same fixed PIU distributions, communication structure, and resource budgets. The table does not pool the additional PIU-distribution conditions or communication structures. For legal Single-Agent Full-Context, the episode-success denominator includes evaluated inputs and structured-interface failures at the final-decision stage, with the latter counted as unsuccessful episodes. Serving-context rejections and other evaluation errors are excluded. When fewer than the fixed inputs contribute to an estimate, the table shows its denominator as n/Nn/N. An em dash in the Single-Agent Full-Context column means that the current archive does not provide a comparable success estimate; it does not convert an unavailable result into a failure.

E.2.0.1 Legal structured-interface failures.

The reported episode success rate is a strict end-to-end measure. We define a structured-interface failure as an episode that does not produce a valid final decision because a participant response or final-decision response cannot be parsed under the required structured response format. A valid final decision is one that is successfully parsed and passed to the problem-specific evaluator. Structured-interface failures remain unsuccessful episodes.

Across the primary legal evaluation, each of the three evaluation conditions contains 1,304 episodes. In 276 multi-agent episodes, a participant response cannot be parsed and the episode terminates before the final-decision stage. Four additional episodes reach the final-decision stage but do not produce a valid final-decision response. Of these 280 structured-interface failures, 254 are produced by the two Claude models: 250 occur during participant interaction and four at the final-decision stage.

The failure records do not support reliable semantic rescoring. For failed responses, the archive retains only the first 500 characters and does not record the complete raw response, provider finish reason, or output-token count. We therefore cannot reliably distinguish schema noncompliance from generation truncation or determine what a model would have produced had generation continued.

Among episodes that produce a valid final decision, the corresponding diagnostic success rates are 75.5%, 55.0%, and 35.1%. The communication and retrieval gaps therefore remain 20.5 and 19.9 percentage points, respectively. These conditional rates are descriptive rather than alternative estimates of end-to-end performance: producing a valid final decision is itself an outcome that can depend on the model and evaluation condition.

As an additional sensitivity analysis, excluding both Claude models gives strict aggregate legal episode success rates of 69.8%, 49.4%, and 32.3% in Single-Agent All-PIU, Multi-Agent PIU-Only, and Multi-Agent Full-Context, respectively. Conditional on producing a valid final decision, the corresponding rates are 69.8%, 49.7%, and 33.0%. The strict gaps are 20.4 and 17.1 percentage points, and the conditional gaps are 20.1 and 16.7 points.

In the additional Single-Agent Full-Context evaluation, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 produce seven and two structured-interface failures, respectively, at the final-decision stage. These evaluated inputs remain unsuccessful episodes; serving-context rejections and other evaluation errors remain excluded from the episode-success denominator as described above.

E.3 Single-Agent Full-Context Evaluation Counts

Some Single-Agent Full-Context model inputs exceed the serving endpoint’s context limit or otherwise fail before evaluation. The current coverage audit spans the 11 source corpora other than DeepSWE; Single-Agent Full-Context was not run for the DeepSWE cohort. Table 32 separately reports evaluated problem-instance–model pairs, context-window failures, output failures, and other unavailable failures across domains. The percentages use all fixed problem-instance–model pairs for each domain–model row as the denominator. Episode-success rates include output failures as unsuccessful episodes but exclude context-window, infrastructure, and judge failures. Table 30 reports the resulting failed/evaluable count and uses an em dash only when no comparable success estimate is available.

Across these 11 source corpora and all models, 2,099 of 2,632 scheduled inputs (79.7%) were normally evaluated, 50 (1.9%) had output failures that remain in the episode-success denominator, 460 (17.5%) exceeded a context window, and 23 (0.9%) had other unavailable failures. Thus, 2,149 inputs contribute to Single-Agent Full-Context episode-success estimates. The Full-Context values reported in Table 30 therefore distinguish episode success from evaluation coverage rather than treating unavailable inputs as incorrect final decisions.

The nine legal Claude entries labeled Output failures in the table, seven for Sonnet and two for Haiku, are structured-interface failures at the final-decision stage, as described in Appendix E.2.0.1, and are included as unsuccessful episodes rather than treated as serving-context rejections.

E.4 Synthesis and Error-Uptake Analysis

This appendix reports the labeling criteria and transcript interventions for correct synthesis and error uptake summarized in Section 4.3.

E.4.1 Definitions and Design

A PIU is faithfully communicated when a participant message preserves its meaning without changing its value, entity, scope, qualification, or effect. An error is an incorrect or unsupported sentence or component that could affect the final decision. Error uptake occurs when a later participant uses an error from a previous visible message to produce a new sentence; rejecting or correcting the earlier error does not count. The intended synthesis criterion is an inference that combines at least two distinct PIUs; repeating one PIU or merely proposing an answer does not count. A synthesis inference is correct when it is supported by the reference PIUs and reference decision. An explicit answer proposal directly states the final choice or requested answer.

The analysis uses 474 frozen Multi-Agent PIU-Only trajectories: 79 problem instances crossed with Round robin, Current-speaker selection, and Simultaneous responses, for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B-A22B participants; Section 4.3 abbreviates the latter as Qwen3-235B. Every participant receives exactly one PIU. A separate GPT-5.5 auditor labels sentence-level components. Participants are not rerun. Instead, we reconstruct the transcript supplied to the final decision maker and regenerate the final decision. The intervention results pool Round robin and Current-speaker selection, giving 158 original trajectories for each participant-model–final-decision-maker combination; intervention effects are paired within trajectory, and confidence intervals are paired 95% bootstrap intervals.

E.4.2 Correct-Synthesis Intervention

For each original transcript TT, let E⁡(T)E(T) contain the reference versions of only the PIUs faithfully communicated in TT. PIUs that are absent or communicated incorrectly are excluded. Let S⁡(T)S(T) contain the correct synthesis claims generated in TT, after removing explicit answer proposals. We compare E⁡(T)E(T) with E⁡(T)+S⁡(T)E(T)+S(T). The two inputs therefore contain the same PIUs and differ only in whether they include correct synthesis.

Correct synthesis improves episode success in all four comparisons. The effect is larger for the Qwen3 final decision maker than for GPT-5.5 for both participant models. Because S⁡(T)S(T) excludes explicit answer proposals, this effect cannot be attributed to direct answer copying.

E.4.2.1 Scope qualification.

The intended synthesis definition requires at least two distinct PIUs. The auditor-labeled set used here also includes some inferences that combine one PIU with information from the publicly visible decision options. Accordingly, the reported effects apply to this broader auditor-labeled set and should not be interpreted as isolating synthesis across distinct PIUs.

E.4.3 Error-Uptake Intervention

The control is the reconstructed original transcript. In the intervention, we remove later sentences produced using an error from a previous visible message, while retaining the sentence containing the original error. This isolates the additional effect of later participants taking up the error. A positive effect means that removing error-uptake sentences improves episode success.

Removing error uptake improves episode success for Qwen3-235B-A22B participants under both final decision makers. The Qwen3-32B estimates have the same sign, but their confidence intervals include zero. These effects are smaller than the corresponding correct-synthesis effects in all four comparisons and do not by themselves explain the communication-structure ordering. We do not apply the error-uptake intervention to Simultaneous responses because participants cannot observe one another; incorrect or inconsistent simultaneous messages are independent rather than propagated errors.

E.4.4 Explicit Answer Proposals

As a separate check, we remove explicit answer proposals from the original Round robin and Current-speaker selection transcripts. The effect is −5.7-5.7 percentage points for Qwen3-32B participants and final decision makers and −10.8-10.8 points for Qwen3-235B-A22B participants and final decision makers. Explicit answer proposals therefore also help the Qwen3 final decision makers. They cannot, however, explain the correct-synthesis results in Table 33, where such proposals are excluded from S⁡(T)S(T).

Overall, adding correct synthesis improves episode success in all four comparisons. Removing error uptake has smaller effects, with confidence intervals excluding zero only for Qwen3-235B-A22B participants. The synthesis effects are smaller with GPT-5.5 than with the Qwen3 final decision makers.

E.5 PIU-Distribution–Communication-Structure Interaction Estimates

Table 35 reports the complete probability-scale interaction estimates from the problem-family and model fixed-effects specifications described in Section 4.4.

For PIU-distribution condition ℓ\ell and communication structure cc, the reported value is the average difference-in-differences in predicted episode success probability:

100​𝔼​[{pe​(ℓ,c)−pe​(ℓ,c0)}−{pe​(ℓ0,c)−pe​(ℓ0,c0)}],100\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\{p_{e}(\ell,c)-p_{e}(\ell,c_{0})\}-\{p_{e}(\ell_{0},c)-p_{e}(\ell_{0},c_{0})\}\right],

where pe​(ℓ,c)p_{e}(\ell,c) is episode ee’s predicted success probability under (ℓ,c)(\ell,c), ℓ0\ell_{0} and c0c_{0} are the PIU-distribution and communication-structure reference categories, and the expectation averages over the evaluated models and problem instances.

E.6 Robustness Analysis with Problem-Instance Fixed Effects

The main analysis in Section 4.4 includes problem-family and model fixed effects. As a stricter within-problem-instance comparison, we replace the problem-family fixed effects with problem-instance fixed effects:

ye∼Bernoulli⁡(pe),logit⁡(pe)=β0+αme+δqe+πℓe+λce+ωℓe,ce.y_{e}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{e}),\qquad\operatorname{logit}(p_{e})=\beta_{0}+\alpha_{m_{e}}+\delta_{q_{e}}+\pi_{\ell_{e}}+\lambda_{c_{e}}+\omega_{\ell_{e},c_{e}}.

Because each problem instance belongs to exactly one problem family, the problem-instance fixed effects absorb the problem-family fixed effects rather than entering the model alongside them. In both analyses, we assign episode success of zero to 3,448 attempted episodes that failed and exclude unavailable cells. The reference categories, weighting, and problem-instance-clustered standard errors are otherwise the same as in the main analysis.

The problem-instance fixed effects absorb differences in absolute difficulty among the evaluated problem instances. The reported interactions therefore compare changes across PIU distributions and communication structures within the same problem instances. The same five positive Multi-Agent PIU-Only interactions and the same two negative Multi-Agent Full-Context interactions have 95% confidence intervals that exclude zero as in the main analysis, with similar point estimates. The positive Pairwise PIU overlap–Round robin interaction in Multi-Agent Full-Context has a 95% confidence interval that excludes zero only with problem-instance fixed effects. The negative One common PIU–Simultaneous responses Multi-Agent PIU-Only interaction has a 95% confidence interval that includes zero with problem-instance fixed effects.

E.7 Interpreting PIU-Distribution–Communication-Structure Interactions

This appendix reports the matched comparisons and interventions accompanying Section 4.4. The cross-domain interaction estimates and problem-instance fixed-effects analysis remain in Appendix E.5 and Appendix E.6. The finance experiments vary what a coordinator query asks the selected participant to communicate, including by appending public PIU category labels for its assigned PIUs and an instruction to report evidence for each. Speaker selection is held fixed in these interventions. The SARA experiments vary who receives private source material and which participant messages the final decision maker sees. These experiments use separate problem-instance sets and do not estimate the fraction of the cross-domain regression interaction attributable to either mechanism. All effects below concern episode success unless stated otherwise; percentage-point estimates are calculated before rounding the displayed rates.

E.7.1 Finance: Design and Query Interventions

The matched communication comparison uses 59 finance problem instances: 30 FinDVer and 29 FinLongDocQA instances. The primary comparison pools Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B-A22B, with the same model used for the participants and the coordinator or separate final decision maker within an episode. The design crosses One PIU per participant and All-but-one PIU concentration with Coordinator-selected speaker and Round robin, giving 472 primary episodes and 118 problem-instance–model pairs per condition. Participants receive private source material. The interaction compares the difference in episode success between Round robin and Coordinator-selected speaker under All-but-one PIU concentration with the same difference under One PIU per participant.

E.7.1.1 Participant descriptions.

The original public participant descriptions summarize a participant’s subject matter or function, without enumerating the public information categories corresponding to its assigned PIUs. These categories describe what the evidence concerns; they do not disclose the evidence itself. Across the 59 problem instances, their mean lengths are 4.41 words under One PIU per participant and 5.10 words under All-but-one PIU concentration. The 54 participants assigned multiple PIUs have six-word descriptions but a mean of 3.43 public information categories (range 2–6). A brief description thus need not indicate every category of evidence available from a participant assigned multiple PIUs.

E.7.1.2 Experimental logic.

The observed communication difference permits two explanations: the coordinator may fail to select a participant assigned a needed PIU, or its query may limit the evidence that the selected participant reports. Near-complete coverage of required participants motivates the second account. Under Coordinator-selected speaker, the selected participant receives a specific query from the coordinator; under Round robin, there is no coordinator query and the participant responds to the whole decision problem. A query covering one PIU may suffice when the participant holds only that PIU, but may omit other assigned PIUs when several are concentrated with it. If this account is correct, broadening the requested evidence should improve episode success more when one selected participant holds multiple PIUs. We therefore change query content while retaining the source episode’s speaker selection.

E.7.1.3 Fixed speaker selection.
