All query interventions operate within Coordinator-selected speaker. The original coordinator query is the task-specific question recorded in the source episode. For each source episode, we replay the recorded sequence of selected participants and the number of responses. The source material, model, PIU distribution, resource budgets, and final-decision procedure are held fixed across query conditions; participant responses and final decisions are regenerated. Original coordinator queries are not regenerated in response to the new participant messages. The resulting effects apply to this fixed sequence, rather than to a coordinator that adapts its later selections or queries.

E.7.1.4 Public information categories in the query.

After speaker selection, one intervention appends a numbered list of the public PIU category labels corresponding to the selected participant’s assigned PIUs and an instruction to report the supporting facts or numbers for each category. The added list contains short public PIU category labels, without private source text, detailed evidence, values, answers, entity scope, or period scope. It augments the original query; it does not replace the participant description or alter speaker selection. For example, an original description is “service proceeds and cybersecurity operations reviewer.” The added list includes service agreement proceeds details, cybersecurity operations exposure, liquidity going-concern assessment, cryptocurrency market exposure, earnings profitability outlook, and share-based compensation expense. These labels specify the topics of the assigned evidence, without supplying the proceeds, expenses, or other private facts needed to answer the problem. Categories need not correspond one-to-one to PIUs: several PIUs may concern the same category.

The added block averages 50.36 words for participants assigned one PIU and 61.00 words for participants assigned multiple PIUs. It is visible to the selected participant and remains in the public transcript. The treatment jointly changes the available category labels and the explicit elicitation instruction; their separate effects are not identified.

The primary comparison with and without these additions contains 59 instances ×\times 2 Qwen3 models ×\times 2 PIU distributions ×\times 2 query conditions ×\times 3 repetitions, or 1,416 episodes. This analysis plan was frozen after an earlier generic-instruction experiment, rather than preregistered before all related evidence was observed.

E.7.1.5 Removing the task-specific query.

To test whether the additions are necessary or removing the narrow query suffices, we replace each original coordinator query with “It is your turn to contribute,” both with and without the public PIU category labels and instruction. This produces 1,416 additional primary episodes. Together with the 1,416 episodes retaining the original queries, the 2×22\times 2 design crosses query retention versus removal with presence versus absence of the additions under each PIU distribution, giving 2,832 episodes. The original-query comparators are reused from the preceding experiment; they are not generated again for the query-removal comparison.

E.7.1.6 Communication-structure interaction with Round robin held fixed.

For each of the four coordinator query conditions, we retain the 236 original Qwen3 Round robin episodes and replace only the Coordinator-selected speaker outcomes with the corresponding repetition-averaged replay outcomes. The intervention operates under both PIU distributions; One PIU per participant controls for a general benefit from changing the query. Let GRG_{R} be the difference in episode success between All-but-one PIU concentration and One PIU per participant under Round robin, and let GC​(k)G_{C}(k) be that difference under Coordinator-selected speaker with query condition kk. In percentage points, the communication-structure interaction is

I⁡(k)=GR−GC​(k).I(k)=G_{R}-G_{C}(k).

The fixed GRG_{R} is −12.7-12.7 points. Consequently, a selective improvement in the concentrated coordinator condition reduces I⁡(k)I(k) by the same amount. This calculation uses the same primary Qwen3 population and adds no episodes. It distinguishes the original single-generation comparison from the three-repetition coordinator replay; their baseline estimates need not be identical. The original Round robin and replay coordinator outcomes are resampled together for inference on each interaction and its change.

E.7.1.7 Budgets, outcomes, and inference.

Follow-up generation uses temperature 0.2, a 40,000-token private-context budget per participant, 600-token participant and coordinator utterance caps, and a 1,200-token final rationale budget. Complete queries including the public PIU category labels and instruction satisfy the existing 600-token cap. A temperature-0 GPT-5.5 evaluator scores episode success and a continuous score on a 0–1 scale. A separate temperature-0 GPT-5.5 semantic evaluation compares each PIU’s reference evidence with its assigned participant’s public messages. Substantive communication requires accurate content-bearing evidence; complete communication additionally requires all key task-relevant elements. Repeating a category label alone does not count.

For both follow-up experiments, three repetitions are averaged within each problem-instance–model–PIU-distribution–query-condition combination. All primary confidence intervals use 20,000 percentile bootstrap draws over the 59 problem-instance clusters, retaining both models and all matched conditions together. For the fixed-Round-robin analysis, each draw recomputes I⁡(k)I(k) and the difference between query conditions. The original communication comparison uses the same cluster-bootstrap procedure. No instance or repetition is excluded based on its observed outcome.

E.7.2 Finance: Results and Process Evidence

The primary communication comparison and query-intervention analyses pool Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B-A22B across the same 59 finance problem instances. The original comparison uses one generation per condition; the query interventions average three repetitions. Table 37 reports the original comparison, and the subsequent analysis recalculates its interaction while holding the original Round robin outcomes fixed.

Required participants speak in 97.2% of cases under One PIU per participant and 99.2% under All-but-one PIU concentration with Coordinator-selected speaker; both Round robin rates are 100%. This weakens an explanation based solely on failing to select a participant assigned a needed PIU.

E.7.2.1 Communication-structure interaction with Round robin held fixed.

Table 38 reports the interaction for each coordinator query condition and its change from the original-query replay. The replay baseline is +15.5+15.5 points (95% CI [3.4,27.4][3.4,27.4]), compared with +13.6+13.6 ([0.8,26.3][0.8,26.3]) in the original comparison. Adding the labels and instruction reduces it by 9.69.6 points; query removal reduces it by 20.920.9 without additions and 24.924.9 with them relative to that same baseline. All three changes exclude zero, while all three residual interaction intervals include zero. The latter does not establish equivalence to zero or a reversal of the communication-structure ordering.

E.7.2.2 Intervention effects within Coordinator-selected speaker.

Table 39 reports success rates in the four query conditions. Table 40 reports PIU-distribution–intervention interactions: each intervention’s success effect under All-but-one PIU concentration minus its effect under One PIU per participant. With the Round robin outcomes held fixed, these effects reduce the communication-structure interaction by the same amount. For query removal with additions, the comparison retains the additions in both conditions; it therefore differs from the combined intervention’s change relative to the original query without additions.

E.7.2.3 Removing the task-specific query.

Query removal improves success more under All-but-one PIU concentration both without and with additions (Table 40). This direction also holds within both source corpora: the intervention interactions without additions are +23.9+23.9 points in FinDVer (95% CI [11.7,36.7][11.7,36.7]) and +17.8+17.8 in FinLongDocQA ([4.0,31.6][4.0,31.6]); with additions, they are +16.7+16.7 ([6.1,26.7][6.1,26.7]) and +13.8+13.8 ([3.4,23.6][3.4,23.6]), respectively.

Without the labels and instruction, the pooled-Qwen3 allocation gap decreases from 28.2 points (95% CI [18.1,38.4][18.1,38.4]) with original coordinator queries to 7.3 points ([−0.6,15.3][-0.6,15.3]) with the coordinator query removed. With the labels and instruction, it decreases from 18.6 points ([10.7,26.8][10.7,26.8]) to 3.4 points ([−3.1,9.3][-3.1,9.3]). These point estimates correspond to 74% and 82% attenuation of the respective original-query allocation gaps. They are not proportions of the original +13.6+13.6-point communication interaction explained. The residual intervals include zero, which does not establish statistical equivalence.

E.7.2.4 Combining the interventions.

The query-removal interaction is +20.9+20.9 points without additions and +15.3+15.3 with them. Their difference, the PIU-distribution–query-removal–additions interaction, is +5.6+5.6 points (95% CI [−4.2,15.5][-4.2,15.5]). Adding labels and an instruction under query removal has an interaction of +4.0+4.0 points ([−4.5,12.4][-4.5,12.4]). Neither interval excludes zero. The combined condition has the smallest allocation gap descriptively, but these comparisons do not establish separate, additive, or synergistic effects of the two interventions.

E.7.2.5 Communicated evidence.

Adding the public PIU category labels and instruction selectively increases substantive PIU communication under All-but-one PIU concentration relative to One PIU per participant, with an interaction of +6.3+6.3 points (95% CI [4.0,8.8][4.0,8.8]); the complete-communication interaction is +3.6+3.6 points ([0.3,7.1][0.3,7.1]). Query removal yields substantive communication interactions of +9.5+9.5 points without the labels and instruction ([5.7,13.5][5.7,13.5]) and +8.5+8.5 with the labels and instruction ([5.8,11.3][5.8,11.3]). The corresponding participant-word-count interactions are +4.3+4.3 words per response ([−0.1,8.6][-0.1,8.6]) and −6.3-6.3 ([−11.7,−1.3][-11.7,-1.3]). Thus, selective improvement in substantive communication does not require selectively longer responses in both comparisons.

E.7.2.6 Supporting qualitative audit.

An outcome-selected audit covers all three actor models, including GPT-5.5. It examines the 47 original problem-instance–model pairs in which Coordinator-selected speaker failed and Round robin succeeded under All-but-one PIU concentration. A temperature-0 GPT-5.5 auditor saw both concentrated transcripts and the corresponding One PIU per participant transcripts. Condition names and success labels were withheld, while transcript structure remained visible. The auditor attributed the primary difference to queries limiting response scope in 44 pairs and to a mixture of mechanisms in three. These selected frequencies are supporting process evidence, rather than population mechanism frequencies or causal mediation estimates.

E.7.2.7 Selected episode.

For an HLI 2024 10-Q problem instance with Qwen3-235B-A22B, the original coordinator query asked about Financial Restructuring fee recognition. The selected participant also held evidence about acquisition consideration, income-tax factors, and the quarterly compensation ratio. Its five PIUs corresponded to four public information categories, since two concerned fee recognition. The added list named these categories and the instruction requested evidence for each; it did not supply the facts reported below. Without the public PIU category labels and instruction, two of five PIUs were substantively communicated in all three repetitions and all final decisions failed. With the public PIU category labels and instruction, all five were communicated, including the 63.4% compensation ratio, the tax-rate change from 20.2% to 26.9% and its explanation, and acquisition consideration of $14.5M plus $4.0M. All three final decisions succeeded. This selected episode illustrates the intervention; the effect estimates use all 59 problem instances.

E.7.2.8 Scope.

The fixed-selection interventions identify effects of query content on participant communication and episode success. They do not show that richer participant descriptions improve the coordinator’s selection or its initially generated query. The public PIU category labels and instruction are supplied after selection and their effects are not separated. The design does not separate their effect on the selected participant from their effect on later readers of the transcript. Holding the original Round robin outcomes fixed permits direct estimation of changes in the communication-structure interaction within the same Qwen3 population. The appropriate baseline is the original-query replay, rather than the original single-generation coordinator outcomes. These results support a role for query content in the interaction, but do not establish complete causal mediation, equivalence of the residual interaction to zero, or generalization to an adaptive coordinator or the cross-domain regression.

E.7.3 SARA: Source-Material and Transcript Interventions

Three experiments use the same 45 SARA problem instances and Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, and GPT-5.5. The longest instance, sara_subproof_tax_case_90_taxable_income, was designated for development checks and excluded from all primary analyses, leaving 44 problem instances. Each configuration is repeated three times. Within an episode, participants and the coordinator or separate final decision maker use the same model. All actors see public participant descriptions generated from public information categories that identify the subject matter without revealing private facts or answers. The descriptions contain 3–6 words (mean 3.72). Their availability is held fixed; the experiments do not estimate their causal effect or whether every actor uses them correctly.

Under One PIU per participant, every participant is assigned one PIU. Under All-but-one PIU concentration, two participants receive all PIUs; the others receive none. The participant assigned all but one receives 5–11 PIUs (mean 7.73), and 4–10 participants per instance receive none (mean 6.71). Participant messages have a 600-token cap and private contexts have a 24,000-token cap per participant. Actor temperature is 0.2; episode-success and semantic evaluation use GPT-5.5 at temperature 0. Speaker order and initial speaker are fixed within problem instance, PIU distribution, and repetition, and reused across models and evidence conditions. The participant assigned all but one PIU speaks first in only 16 of 132 primary concentrated-allocation instance–repetition combinations.

E.7.3.1 Exact PIUs with or without source material.

Source material may impair the processing of participants assigned PIUs, or generate additional messages from participants assigned no PIU that impair the final decision. To examine these pathways, we compare Multi-Agent PIU-Only with a condition that adds the original private source material. In both conditions, participants receive their assigned PIUs explicitly as facts relevant to the decision; the added-source condition also supplies source material to participants assigned no PIU. This tests whether source material changes the interaction when the relevant facts are already supplied directly. In Multi-Agent Full-Context, participants instead receive source material from which they must retrieve their assigned PIUs. Explicit availability does not ensure that participants communicate or use the facts correctly. The comparison crosses two PIU distributions, all five communication structures, and these two evidence conditions. The complete design contains 8,100 episodes (45 instances ×\times 3 models ×\times 2 evidence conditions ×\times 2 PIU distributions ×\times 5 structures ×\times 3 repetitions), with 7,920 primary episodes over 44 instances.

For communication structure cc and evidence condition vv, define

A⁡(v,c)=100​{Success⁡(All-but-one,v,c)−Success⁡(One PIU per participant,v,c)}.A(v,c)=100\{\operatorname{Success}(\text{All-but-one},v,c)-\operatorname{Success}(\text{One PIU per participant},v,c)\}.

The source-material interaction is A⁡(PIUs and source material,c)−A⁡(Multi-Agent PIU-Only,c)A(\text{PIUs and source material},c)-A(\text{Multi-Agent PIU-Only},c). A negative value means that source material makes PIU concentration more harmful relative to One PIU per participant under that structure.

The communication-structure interaction compares these allocation effects:

I⁡(v)=A⁡(v,Simultaneous responses)−A⁡(v,Coordinator-selected speaker).I(v)=A(v,\text{Simultaneous responses})-A(v,\text{Coordinator-selected speaker}).

The change reported in Section 4.4.2 is I⁡(PIUs and source material)−I⁡(Multi-Agent PIU-Only)I(\text{PIUs and source material})-I(\text{Multi-Agent PIU-Only}). It therefore compares the source-material interactions between the two communication structures, rather than reporting the interaction within Simultaneous responses alone.

E.7.3.2 Who receives source material.

The preceding comparison changes source-material access for both groups together. It therefore cannot distinguish a loss originating with participants assigned PIUs from one originating with participants assigned no PIU. The source-material intervention independently varies source-material access for the two participants assigned PIUs and for the participants assigned no PIU under All-but-one PIU concentration. Exact PIUs, public descriptions, models, repetitions, and speaker order remain fixed. We compare no added source material, source material for participants assigned PIUs only, source material for participants assigned no PIU only, and source material for both groups. The experiment covers Coordinator-selected speaker, Broadcast query, and Simultaneous responses, generating 2,430 new episodes, of which 2,376 concern the 44 primary instances. The no-source and both-group conditions reuse the preceding comparison. Under One PIU per participant, there are no participants assigned no PIU, so the corresponding source-material conditions are identical rather than independent additional observations.

E.7.3.3 Which messages reach the final decision maker.

Source-material placement changes a participant’s local processing and public messages together. Even if source material for participants assigned no PIU causes the larger loss, this does not establish whether their messages impair final synthesis. If the loss is transmitted through those messages, hiding them only at the final-decision stage should improve episode success when their authors receive source material, with little improvement when they do not. The transcript intervention tests this prediction using frozen All-but-one PIU concentration–Simultaneous responses trajectories from the condition with no added source material and the condition with source material only for participants assigned no PIU. For each trajectory, the final decision maker receives either the complete transcript or only messages from the two participants assigned PIUs. Participant messages, descriptions, PIU assignment, and speaker order remain fixed; only the final decision is regenerated. Both visibility conditions use the same replay implementation, rather than comparing newly generated decisions with archived ones. A separate complete-transcript replay checks stability against archived outcomes.

This design contains 1,620 episodes (45 instances ×\times 3 models ×\times 2 source-material conditions ×\times 2 message-visibility conditions ×\times 3 repetitions), with 1,584 primary episodes over 44 instances. The primary interaction is the effect of removing messages from participants assigned no PIU when those participants receive source material minus the same removal effect when they do not. Confidence intervals use bootstrap sampling over problem instances, preserving matched conditions. For the transcript intervention, overall intervals use 5,000 draws and model-specific intervals use 2,500 draws.

E.7.4 SARA: Results and Scope

Adding source material makes concentration additionally harmful under four communication structures; the Coordinator-selected speaker interval includes zero. The Simultaneous responses–Coordinator-selected speaker communication-structure interaction is +10.6+10.6 points in Multi-Agent PIU-Only (95% CI [2.3,19.0][2.3,19.0]) and −5.1-5.1 with added source material ([−13.6,3.0][-13.6,3.0]). The change is −15.7-15.7 points ([−26.8,−4.3][-26.8,-4.3]): the −14.1-14.1-point source-material interaction under Simultaneous responses minus the +1.5+1.5-point interaction under Coordinator-selected speaker, calculated before rounding. The negative point estimate in the added-source condition alone does not establish an ordering reversal with statistical confidence, since its interval includes zero.

The interaction is not accompanied by a corresponding reduction in semantic completeness of communicated PIUs. Source-material interactions in completeness are −0.5-0.5 points for Coordinator-selected speaker, +2.2+2.2 for Broadcast query, +1.0+1.0 for Round robin, +3.5+3.5 for Current-speaker selection, and +2.8+2.8 for Simultaneous responses. This motivates a test of information reaching the final decision maker in addition to the participants’ communication of assigned PIUs.

E.7.4.1 Source-material recipients.

Table 43 localizes the larger loss to source material supplied to participants assigned no PIU. Under Simultaneous responses, supplying only that group with source material reduces episode success by 47.2 points (95% CI [−55.3,−39.1][-55.3,-39.1]). Supplying only participants assigned PIUs reduces it by 14.9 points ([−23.0,−7.1][-23.0,-7.1]). Once participants assigned no PIU receive source material, adding it for participants assigned PIUs changes episode success by +0.8+0.8 points ([−3.0,4.3][-3.0,4.3]). Source material for participants assigned no PIU also has the larger negative point estimate under the two coordinator structures; the size of that difference is not itself tested here.

E.7.4.2 Transcript intervention.

Table 44 reports newly generated final decisions under both message-visibility conditions. Removing messages from participants assigned no PIU improves episode success by 47.7 points when those participants receive source material (95% CI [38.9,56.3][38.9,56.3]), compared with −1.0-1.0 points when they do not ([−5.3,3.3][-5.3,3.3]). The interaction is +48.7+48.7 points ([38.9,58.6][38.9,58.6]). After removal, the added-source minus no-source difference is 0.0 points ([−3.8,3.8][-3.8,3.8]). This is consistent with recovery to the Multi-Agent PIU-Only performance level, but does not establish exact equality.

The interaction is positive for every model: +25.0+25.0 points for Qwen3-32B (95% CI [9.1,40.9][9.1,40.9]), +65.2+65.2 for Qwen3-235B-A22B ([51.5,78.0][51.5,78.0]), and +56.1+56.1 for GPT-5.5 ([43.2,67.8][43.2,67.8]). Complete-transcript replay changes episode success relative to archived decisions by only +0.3+0.3 points without added source material ([−2.8,3.3][-2.8,3.3]) and −1.3-1.3 with it ([−3.8,1.5][-3.8,1.5]), supporting stability of the original difference under final-decision regeneration.

Under Simultaneous responses, total message volume from participants assigned no PIU increases from approximately 371 tokens per transcript without source material to 1,396 with source material only for that group. The messages from participants assigned PIUs remain approximately 204 tokens per transcript in both conditions. These are pooled group totals, rather than per-message lengths, and therefore can exceed the 600-token participant cap. The transcript intervention retains the messages communicating assigned PIUs while removing the messages through which source material supplied to the other participants reaches the final decision maker.

E.7.4.3 Scope.

The transcript intervention identifies a harmful contribution of messages from participants assigned no PIU at the final-decision stage, under All-but-one PIU concentration and Simultaneous responses. It does not separate transcript length, distracting content, contradictory reasoning, and the final model’s allocation of attention. It directly tests source material supplied only to participants assigned no PIU; it does not establish the same removal effect when all participants receive source material or under other communication structures. Nor does it imply that contributions from participants assigned no PIU are generally unhelpful. Because the follow-ups supply exact PIUs as well as source material, they support a mechanism relevant to the cross-domain Full-Context pattern without constituting a direct re-estimation or complete causal explanation of that regression interaction.

E.8 Legal Token-Budget Ablations: Complete Results and Diagnostics

For space, Section 4.5 summarizes the principal findings and defers the complete token-budget analyses to this appendix. We preserve the full results presentation below, followed by additional implementation details, budget-binding diagnostics, and results by model and source corpus.

E.8.1 Complete Results Deferred from Section 4.5

We study private-note, message, and local-transcript token budgets under Multi-Agent Full-Context with One PIU per participant and Coordinator-selected speaker. For a problem instance with NN participants, every budget setting permits NN participant messages before the final decision. We hold the coordinator policy and final-decision token budget fixed.

E.8.1.1 Private-note and message token budgets.

Each participant message is generated in two stages. The participant first forms a private working note from its initial local observation and local transcript. A second stage receives the note and the same local transcript and produces the message added to the communication transcript; the note is not shared. The message token budget makes the departure from A3 explicit. Because participants receive source material containing their PIUs rather than the PIUs alone, they must identify the information needed for a correct final decision before producing bounded messages, a requirement related to A2. We cross private-note token budgets of 64, 128, and 256 tokens with message token budgets of 32, 64, 128, and 256 tokens. Table 45 reports GPT-5.5 results over 24 CUAD and 29 Multi-LexSum problem instances; Section E.8.2 provides the complete implementation and results by model and source corpus.

E.8.1.2 Local-transcript token budgets.

We separately limit the newly available message text in each participant’s local transcript. This limit is motivated by work on limited human attention and working memory (Kahneman, 1973; Cowan, 2001), without assuming that language models share the same cognitive mechanisms. We compare first-in, first-out (FIFO) and random contiguous-window reading with GPT-5.5 on the 29 Multi-LexSum problem instances. Section E.8.3 provides the complete implementation and reports how often the token budgets bind.

Private-note tokens Message tokens
32 64 128 256
64 45.3 ±\pm 6.8 67.9 ±\pm 6.4 71.7 ±\pm 6.2 69.8 ±\pm 6.3
128 60.4 ±\pm 6.7 69.8 ±\pm 6.3 81.1 ±\pm 5.4 75.5 ±\pm 5.9
256 60.4 ±\pm 6.7 67.9 ±\pm 6.4 83.0 ±\pm 5.2 81.1 ±\pm 5.4

Table 45 shows the largest gains as the message token budget increases from 32 to 128 tokens. Averaged across private-note token budgets, episode success rate rises from 55.3% to 78.6%, but does not improve further with 256 message tokens; variation across private-note token budgets is smaller than variation across message token budgets.

Figure 12 shows no monotonic relationship between the local-transcript token budget and episode success rate. FIFO remains within 6.9 percentage points of the unlimited baseline, whereas the random-window mean at 16 tokens is 10.3 points lower. Thus, these problem instances do not show a uniform performance penalty from a smaller local-transcript token budget.

E.8.2 Private-Note and Message Token Budgets

For a problem instance with NN participants, Coordinator-selected speaker permits NN participant messages followed by the coordinator’s final decision. Each participant message uses two model generations with the same local transcript. The first generation receives the participant’s initial local observation and produces a private working note. The second receives that note, but not the initial local observation, and produces the message added to the communication transcript. The private working note is not added to the communication transcript or shown to another decision maker.

The experiment crosses private-note token budgets of 64, 128, and 256 tokens with message token budgets of 32, 64, 128, and 256 tokens. The token budget for each participant’s initial local observation is 40,000 tokens, and participant access to the communication transcript is not limited. The coordinator policy and final-decision token budget remain fixed. The 256-token message condition is the largest evaluated message token budget within each private-note row; the grid does not include an unlimited-message condition.

The imposed limits bind as intended. GPT-5.5 participant messages are truncated in approximately 93%, 57%, 23%, and less than 1% of episodes as the message token budget increases, while private-note truncation falls from 82% to 4%. Qwen3-32B does not show a consistent relationship between either token budget and episode success rate. Table 46 reports the source-corpus-specific results for both models.

E.8.3 Local-Transcript Token Budgets

When a participant is selected to send a message, its current directed coordinator query is read first and charged to the local-transcript token budget. Any remaining capacity is used to read previously unread message text. FIFO reading exposes the earliest unread tokens. Random contiguous-window reading instead selects one contiguous window from the previously unread message text, reproducibly for a fixed problem instance, participant, message, and seed. Unread message text remains available when that participant is next selected. The participant also retains its initial local observation, its prior messages, and every local-transcript excerpt it has previously read. The coordinator’s observation is not limited and therefore contains the complete communication transcript.

We fix the private-note and message token budgets at 256 and 128 tokens and compare local-transcript token budgets of 16, 32, 64, and 128 tokens with unlimited reading. A 256-token condition provides an additional check at the largest evaluated token budget. FIFO is evaluated once and random contiguous-window reading is evaluated with three seeds. Accordingly, Table 47 reports binomial standard errors over the 29 fixed problem instances for FIFO and standard deviations across the three episode-success rates for random reading.

The local-transcript token budget binds at every participant message with budgets of 16 and 32 tokens and at approximately 95%, 90%, and 83% of participant messages with budgets of 64, 128, and 256 tokens. At 16 tokens, the coordinator query consumes the complete local-transcript token budget, so FIFO and random contiguous-window reading expose the same prefix; their observed difference reflects run-to-run model variation, not a different selected excerpt. The 256-token condition reaches 86.2% under FIFO and 82.8 ±\pm 6.9% under random reading. Together with the non-monotonic results in Figure 12, these diagnostics do not support a monotonic relationship between the local-transcript token budget and episode success rate on these problem instances.

E.9 Trajectory Examples

We present two representative episode trajectories that illustrate how PIUs move from participants’ initial local observations into the communication transcript and final decision.

E.9.1 Dependency Case and Episode Trajectory: CVS 2022

E.9.1.1 Problem and dependency structure.

This representative FinLongDocQA problem asks for the ratio of CVS Health’s unique digital customers to 2022 revenue in each of three segments, expressed as millions of customers per $1 billion of revenue, and then asks which segment has the largest ratio. Under the One PIU per participant condition, Participant A holds the common customer count, while Participants B–D each hold one segment denominator.

PIU ID PIU Participant assigned the PIU Answer components using the PIU
1 47M unique digital customers Participant A Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4
2 Health Care Benefits revenue: $91.4B Participant B Q1, Q4
3 Pharmacy Services revenue: $169.2B Participant C Q2, Q4
4 Retail revenue: $106.6B Participant D Q3, Q4

The PIUs used by the four answer components are therefore

Q1={1,2},Q2={1,3},Q3={1,4},Q4={1,2,3,4}.Q_{1}=\{1,2\},\qquad Q_{2}=\{1,3\},\qquad Q_{3}=\{1,4\},\qquad Q_{4}=\{1,2,3,4\}.

Counting references component by component gives ten PIU uses, but only four distinct PIUs. No participant can compute even one requested ratio alone, and the final comparison requires all four PIUs.

E.9.1.2 Reference calculation.

Using the same 47M company-wide customer count as the numerator for each requested segment calculation gives

4791.4=0.51,47169.2=0.28,47106.6=0.44.\frac{47}{91.4}=0.51,\qquad\frac{47}{169.2}=0.28,\qquad\frac{47}{106.6}=0.44.

Thus Health Care Benefits has the highest ratio, at 0.51M unique digital customers per $1B of revenue.

E.9.1.3 Observed success by evaluation condition.

The table below reports the result for this problem instance under each model and evaluation condition. A check means that all four answer components were satisfied; a cross means that all four were missing in the final decision.

Model Single-Agent All-PIU Multi-Agent PIU-Only Multi-Agent Full-Context
Claude Sonnet 4.5 ✓\checkmark ✓\checkmark ✓\checkmark
Claude Haiku 4.5 ✓\checkmark ×\times ×\times
E.9.1.4 Successful episode trajectory: Sonnet 4.5.

In Single-Agent All-PIU, the model directly read the four facts, computed 0.51, 0.28, and 0.44, and selected Health Care Benefits. In both multi-agent conditions, all four PIUs entered the communication transcript in the responses to the first four coordinator queries: A disclosed 47M; B disclosed $91.4B; C disclosed $169.2B; and D disclosed $106.6B. The coordinator used the same company-wide customer count in all three ratios, performed the divisions, and returned the same ranking. The semantic judge found all four answer components correct and grounded in all three conditions.

E.9.1.5 Failure episode trajectory 1: Haiku 4.5, Multi-Agent PIU-Only.

The coordinator issued 15 queries to A–D, but every participant response was empty. No PIU entered the communication transcript. The final decision explicitly refused to calculate because it lacked the customer count and segment revenues. The final decision consequently omitted all four answer components. This is a communication failure rather than an arithmetic failure: the same model solved the problem in Single-Agent All-PIU.

E.9.1.6 Failure episode trajectory 2: Haiku 4.5, Multi-Agent Full-Context.

Participant A found the consolidated 47M customer count, but initially reported that the needed segment table was unavailable. Participant C then incorrectly attached $169.2B to Health Care Benefits and could not recover the other two denominators; later participant messages converged on the claim that the accessible excerpts were insufficient. After 15 coordinator queries, the coordinator returned “unable to complete” instead of the three ratios. The final decision omitted all four answer components. Here the source material created an evidence-retrieval and fact-mapping failure even though every PIU remained present in the source material provided to its assigned participant.

E.9.1.7 Case-study implication.

The evaluation holds the problem instance fixed while exposing two distinct collaboration bottlenecks. Multi-Agent PIU-Only can fail because a PIU in a participant’s initial local observation never enters the communication transcript; Multi-Agent Full-Context can fail because relevant facts are lost or misassigned within much longer source material. In Single-Agent All-PIU, both models solve the problem instance when the PIUs are centralized.

E.9.2 Composite-Problem Episode Trajectory: Kirkland’s 2023

E.9.2.1 Generation is not execution.

This representative FinDVer problem contains six questions, but Q1–Q5 are not generated during the episode and Q6 is not appended afterward. All six questions, their links to PIUs, the reference decision, and the PIU distribution are frozen together as one composite problem instance before evaluation. The episode tests whether a coordinator can recover and combine that already-fixed evidence.

Data generation: 10-K source →\rightarrow candidate units →\rightarrow six PIUs →\rightarrow Q1–Q5 analyses and Q6 synthesis →\rightarrow verification of the links between answer components and PIUs →\rightarrow PIU distribution →\rightarrow retained problem instance.

Evaluation execution: initial common observation →\rightarrow coordinator queries →\rightarrow evidence accumulates in the communication transcript →\rightarrow Q1–Q5 and Q6 final decision →\rightarrow answer-component correctness and grounding judgment.

The construction question is therefore “which facts must jointly determine the reference decision?”; the evaluation question is “can the model find those facts and combine only what the filing supports?”

E.9.2.2 From filing disclosures to one analyst problem.

The six-PIU problem joins four review axes that an equity or credit analyst would normally consider together.

Review axis Filing evidence Composite item
Supply chain Sourcing diversification and country-of-origin mix Q1
Profitability 310-bp gross-margin improvement and drivers Q2
Execution risk Capital constraints and tightly managed cash flow Q3
Financing Term-loan terms, balance-date status, later draws Q4–Q5
Integrated judgment Operating improvement plus liquidity pressure Q6

Q6 asks whether the complete narrative is fully supported: Kirkland’s was improving operations through sourcing diversification and gross-margin improvement, while still facing liquidity pressure and using new financing as it executed a financial turnaround strategy. This is not a vote over Q1–Q5; it combines evidence with different scopes and dates into one bounded filing interpretation.

E.9.2.3 Distributed evidence discovery, queries 1–6.

Every participant had the generic participant description “financial filing context reviewer,” so the coordinator initially did not know the PIU-ownership mapping.

Query Participant Item Evidence recovered
1 A Q4 No term-loan balance at Feb. 3; $34M credit borrowing
2 B Q1 Diversification and fiscal 2023 country mix
3 C Q3, Q5 Tight cash management; later $6M and $5M draws
4 D Q3 Capital shortage could limit strategic execution
5 E Q4 $12M term loan; at least $5M initial draw required
6 F Q2 310-bp margin improvement, drivers, and offset

Query 1 illustrates genuine discovery rather than replay of a reference-decision ordering. The coordinator asked A for sourcing information, but A did not own that PIU. A instead disclosed its financing evidence. The coordinator used the updated communication transcript to query another reviewer for the still-missing sourcing component, and recovered all six PIUs by query 6.

E.9.2.4 Cross-source consistency checks, queries 7–15.

Once the decision-relevant facts were present, the remaining questions tested how strongly they could be connected. F confirmed that its margin paragraph did not itself call the improvement part of the financial turnaround. E confirmed that its term-loan-terms paragraph did not state a strategic use of proceeds. By contrast, C’s paragraph jointly disclosed later borrowing, tightly managed cash flow, and execution of the financial turnaround strategy. The defensible synthesis is therefore that the company used additional financing while executing the turnaround under cash pressure–not that a particular loan directly caused or funded a particular operating improvement.

E.9.2.5 Successful three-stage episode trajectory: Sonnet 4.5, Multi-Agent PIU-Only.

1. Distributed evidence discovery: queries 1–6 mapped the six anonymous reviewers to sourcing, margin, capital-risk, term-loan, balance-date, and post-year-end evidence. 2. Checking support for cross-passage conclusions: queries 7–15 distinguished direct filing statements from unsupported cross-passage inferences and preserved the February 3 balance-date versus subsequent-borrowing distinction. 3. Integrated conclusion: the final decision reported Q1–Q5 and concluded that Q6 was fully supported. The episode used the complete budget of 15 participant responses, and all six answer components were correct and grounded.

E.9.2.6 Efficiency and interpretation.

The episode trajectory is deliberately informative rather than optimal. An initial misdirected query was necessary because PIU ownership was hidden, whereas several queries after query 6 repeated checks of whether the filing supported the proposed cross-passage conclusions after the core facts were already complete. For presentation, the 15 coordinator queries and responses are most clearly compressed into the three stages above. The example then shows more than parallel subproblem solving: it shows distributed evidence recovery, verification of permissible cross-source links, and construction of one realistic operational-and-liquidity judgment.

Appendix F Literature Motivation for the PIU-Distribution–Communication-Structure Interaction

Section 4.4 tests whether differences in episode success rate between communication structures change across PIU distributions. Three complementary literatures motivate this comparison and the interaction specification.

F.0.0.1 Team decision-making under a decentralized information structure.

Team decision theory studies decision makers who pursue a shared objective but have different information available to them (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Nayyar et al., 2013). This is the basic structure of our evaluation conditions with multiple participants: the participants share the episode objective, while PIU distribution determines which PIUs are available to which participants. Consistent with this formulation, we hold the problem instance and model fixed while varying PIU distribution. The literature does not imply that a particular PIU distribution must perform best, because performance also depends on whether the distributed PIUs enter communication and support a correct final decision.

F.0.0.2 Communication under a decentralized information structure.

Communication complexity and distributed-function computation study how separately informed parties exchange the information needed to compute a shared target (Yao, 1979; Orlitsky and Roche, 2001). Work on knowledge in distributed systems likewise formalizes communication as changing the information available to decision makers (Halpern and Moses, 1990). In our setting, communication structure determines who may send a message at each point in the episode and which earlier messages that participant can observe, while PIU distribution determines where the relevant information is initially available. We study PIU distribution and communication structure jointly because differences in episode success rate among communication structures may vary across PIU distributions.

F.0.0.3 PIUs entering communication.

Hidden-profile experiments show that information observed by only one participant may fail to enter group discussion (Stasser and Titus, 1985). This evidence is directly relevant to PIU distributions that place a PIU with only one participant or concentrate multiple PIUs with one participant. It also explains why the proportion of participants who send a message is not by itself sufficient: episode success depends on whether the communication structure elicits and preserves the PIUs needed for a correct final decision.

F.0.0.4 Implications for the empirical specification.

The specification includes PIU-distribution and communication-structure main effects and their interaction, allowing differences among communication structures to vary across PIU distributions. Because both are represented as categorical conditions and every non-reference pair receives an interaction term, the specification does not impose that their relationships with episode success are independent. The Bernoulli model and logit link reflect that episode success is binary, while problem-family and model fixed effects adjust for differences across problem families and models. Standard errors are clustered by problem instance, and Appendix E.6 reports the stricter specification with problem-instance fixed effects. The analysis estimates empirical relationships among the evaluated conditions; these literatures motivate the comparison but do not make the interaction estimates causal tests of any one theory.

Appendix G Policy-Training Data, Evaluation, and Diagnostic Analyses

This appendix documents the data, evaluation, training configurations, and diagnostic analyses for the two policy-training demonstrations in Section 5. We first describe the CUAD-derived and MAUD-derived free-form decisions and their evaluator. We then report the demonstration under Coordinator-selected speaker and the demonstration under Current-speaker selection, with the participant that ends communication making the final decision.

G.0.0.1 Relation to assumptions A1, A2, and A3.

Both demonstrations address A1 by training and comparing language-model policy collections rather than assuming that a jointly optimal policy collection is available before execution. The Coordinator-selected speaker demonstration additionally departs from A2 because participants derive messages from source material, whereas the Current-speaker selection demonstration provides PIUs directly. Both demonstrations depart from A3 by enforcing explicit observation and communication budgets.

G.1 Free-Form Legal Decisions and Evaluation

G.1.1 Construction and Data Splits

We construct CUAD-derived and MAUD-derived problem instances from the corresponding distributed CUAD and MAUD problem instances while preserving the PIU distribution and source material. For each input problem instance, GPT-5.5 receives the original decision task, the reasoning supporting its reference decision, the PIUs and their source text, and the PIU distribution. It produces a standalone legal question, a source-grounded reference decision, PIU-grounded answer components, a component requiring synthesis across all PIUs, material contradictions that disqualify a final decision, and problem-specific evaluation criteria. The question identifies the dimensions to resolve without exposing the original decision alternatives or their labels.

A separate GPT-5.5 call first checks the proposed question, reference decision, and evaluation criteria against the source evidence. The check rejects disguised multiple choice, reference-decision leakage, questions answerable from one PIU, unsupported content, incomplete PIU coverage, and criteria that would accept a partial or vague final decision. Deterministic checks then enforce the length and format requirements, require at least one answer component grounded in every PIU and one component synthesizing all PIUs, and verify that the PIU distribution is unchanged. If either stage fails, the proposal is revised using the resulting findings. Of 396 retained problem instances, 283 pass on the first draft; the remaining instances require up to seven revision rounds.

Across the 396 problem instances, the PIU count has median 2, mean 2.13, and range 2–6. Questions contain 47 words at the median, and reference decisions contain 100 words at the median. On the 62 CUAD-derived validation and MAUD-derived evaluation instances, the evaluator receives a median of six answer components: five grounded in individual PIUs and one requiring cross-PIU synthesis. All 62 reference decisions receive an LLM-judged score of 1.0. By contrast, 62 single-PIU partial decisions and 62 original incorrect decision alternatives have a mean score of 0.193. Policies never observe the reference decisions, answer-component annotations, PIU identifiers, construction checks, or evaluation criteria.

G.1.2 GPT-5.5 Evaluator

Free-form decisions admit multiple valid surface forms, so the evaluator compares a candidate final decision with the reference decision, PIUs, answer components, problem-specific evaluation criteria, and material contradictions. GPT-5.5 directly assigns an LLM-judged score in [0,1][0,1]. The implementation clips the returned value to this interval and assigns zero when the score is unavailable. The arithmetic mean across problem instances is the reported LLM-judged score and the only semantic training reward. The evaluation criteria require the final decision to reach the reference conclusion, cover the required content, satisfy the applicable numeric and legal conditions, and contain no disqualifying error. A malformed or missing judge response receives a score of zero. All evaluations use the AWS Bedrock-hosted GPT-5.5 at temperature zero with the same prompt and normalization procedure.

G.2 Coordinator-selected speaker: Participant and Coordinator Policy Training

All episodes in this subsection use Multi-Agent Full-Context with Coordinator-selected speaker. A shared participant policy generates bounded messages from each selected participant’s initial local observation, while a coordinator policy generates coordinator queries and the final decision. Each initial local observation has a 28,000-token budget; participant messages have a 48-token budget within a 64-token structured completion; coordinator queries have a 64-token budget; and the final decision has a 256-token budget within a 384-token structured completion. Participants do not generate private notes.

G.2.1 Optimization and Training Configurations

Each update samples eight shuffled CUAD-derived training problem instances and eight rollouts per problem instance, yielding 64 episode rollouts. GRPO standardizes the eight rewards within each problem instance and broadcasts the resulting episode advantage to the trainable actions. An invalid trainable action instead receives a local advantage of −0.1-0.1 and one retry. We update all parameters of each trainable policy with AdamW for one epoch per update using a PPO-style clipped surrogate, ratio clip 0.2, dual-clip bound 3.0 for negative advantages, sequence-mean/token-mean loss aggregation, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, weight decay 0.01, and a 10−310^{-3} KL loss relative to the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct policy. Training runs for 80 updates, validation occurs every 10 updates with greedy decoding, and each configuration uses four H200 GPUs.

The LLM-judged score is the training reward in all configurations. Which participant the coordinator queries, query order, which PIUs appear in participant messages, and whether the coordinator queries every participant do not enter the reward.

G.2.2 Two-Stage Policy Training

The participant-only stage updates the participant policy while the base coordinator policy remains fixed. We evaluate the participant policy every 10 updates; the version after update 60 is the first to attain the highest mean LLM-judged score on CUAD-derived validation and is therefore used in the coordinator-only continuation. This continuation initializes the coordinator policy from the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct policy and holds the trained participant policy fixed. The coordinator policy selected after this stage is the update-80 checkpoint.

The participant-policy comparison uses episodes generated by the base and trained participant policies under the same fixed coordinator policy and decoding configuration. Table 51 shows that training causes participant messages to include information needed for a correct final decision and changes which PIUs appear across participant messages. In the insurance-obligations example, the trained participant policy produces a different first message. Although the coordinator policy remains fixed, it consequently observes a different transcript and queries participant B instead of repeating participant A.

The coordinator-policy comparison holds the trained participant policy fixed. Table 52 shows one example in which changed coordinator queries cause participant messages to include both the certificate-on-request clause and a reciprocal insurance obligation. In another, the trained coordinator policy produces the correct final decision from participant messages that are substantively unchanged. These examples separate changes arising from participant messages from changes arising through coordinator queries or the final decision.

On the 26 MAUD-derived problem instances held out from training and checkpoint selection, two-stage policy training does not improve the aggregate LLM-judged score.

G.2.3 Joint Two-Policy Training

Joint two-policy training removes weight sharing between the participant and coordinator policies. Both policies are initialized independently from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, maintain separate optimizer states and clipped-surrogate losses, and receive the same team payoff. Every update has a nonzero gradient norm for each policy, ruling out the failure mode in which one shared policy generates or updates both participant and coordinator actions.

The reported run uses random seed 29, 80 updates, and 5,120 episode rollouts. The update-80 pair attains the highest mean LLM-judged score among the scheduled CUAD-derived validation evaluations. The score increases from 11.97% to 22.38%. The coordinator queries every participant on 100% of validation problem instances by update 20 and maintains that rate through update 80.

The coordinator-query diagnostics use one greedy rollout per CUAD-derived validation problem instance. A first query copies the problem question only when the query and question match after normalization for case, punctuation, and whitespace. A later query is lexically reply-conditioned when it contains an explicit follow-up marker or at least two terms from a preceding participant message that are absent from the problem question. This diagnostic does not constitute a causal test of adaptation. The trained coordinator queries every participant, uses short queries, and does not copy the problem question in the first query; lexically reply-conditioned later queries remain infrequent. Thus, the learned coordinator-query behavior is distinguished by querying every participant with short queries, rather than by a high rate of lexically reply-conditioned later queries.

In one CUAD-derived validation example, the base participant and coordinator policies elicit only the parties and the Type I material label and produce a one-directional final decision with an LLM-judged score of 12.5%. The jointly trained policies instead elicit the IBM-to-Customer Type II permissions from one participant and the Customer-to-IBM downstream-authorization right for Type I materials from another. Their final decision represents both grant directions and receives 62.5%, although it remains incomplete. This example illustrates coordinated evidence decomposition but does not establish that the interaction between the two trained policies is necessary.

Under the jointly trained participant and coordinator policies, the coordinator queries every participant and every participant sends a public message on all 26 MAUD-derived problem instances; both behaviors occur on 20 of 26 instances under the base participant and coordinator policies. The LLM-judged score changes only slightly, from 5.12% to 5.58%. The query and messaging patterns therefore transfer more clearly than task-specific evidence use or final-decision quality.

G.3 Current-speaker selection: Shared Participant Policy Training

G.3.1 Problem Instances and Communication Structure

This experiment uses Multi-Agent PIU-Only with One PIU per participant under Current-speaker selection. The participant that ends communication makes the final decision; there is no separate final decision maker. Training contains 350 FinDVer problem instances with two to eight participants and 188 FinLongDocQA problem instances with two or three participants. Validation contains 39 FinDVer and 21 FinLongDocQA problem instances. The held-out test set contains 40 four-participant FinLongDocQA problem instances. Canonical task identifiers and source-material groups do not overlap across splits. Four-participant FinLongDocQA is absent from training, although four-participant FinDVer occurs in training.

Each participant receives exactly one PIU in its initial local observation. The initial common observation contains the decision objective, decision format, and a directory of participant identifiers and public participant descriptions. The descriptions are short role names generated from the broad subject of the assigned PIU. Deterministic checks and a separate leakage check reject names that expose a value, polarity, condition, conclusion, or decision implication. A prompt-construction check of all 638 normalized instances and 4,988 rendered prompts confirms that every directory contains the permitted participants and that no participant receives another participant’s PIU.

In each round, the current speaker sends a public message and either selects the next participant or ends communication and makes the final decision. If the 15-round communication budget is exhausted, the last speaker makes the final decision. Public messages have a 600-token budget, the final-decision field has a 1,200-token budget, participant actions have 1,200 private reasoning tokens, and the final decision has 1,800 private reasoning tokens. The runtime also applies a 750-token structured-generation cap, a 16,384-token prompt cap, and a 24,576-token training-sequence cap.

G.3.2 Optimization and Checkpoint Selection

A single Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct participant policy is shared across participants. Participant messages, next-participant selection, decisions to end communication, and the final decision all receive participant-policy gradients. Each update samples eight problem instances and 16 rollouts per instance, yielding 128 rollouts per update and 10,240 rollouts across 80 updates. Rollouts use temperature 0.7 and top-p=0.95p=0.95; validation uses greedy decoding.

Training updates all parameters of the shared participant policy using FSDP in bfloat16 on four H200 GPUs. GRPO standardizes the 16 rewards within each problem instance. Invalid JSON, schema-invalid actions, and invalid next-participant identifiers receive a local advantage of −0.1-0.1 and one retry. Optimization uses AdamW with learning rate 10−610^{-6}, weight decay 0.01, gradient-norm clip 1.0, PPO ratio clip 0.2, dual-clip bound 3.0 for negative advantages, and sequence-mean/token-mean loss aggregation. This run does not use a KL loss.

Checkpoint selection uses the mean LLM-judged score on the 39 FinDVer validation problem instances, with the earlier update winning a tie. The 21 FinLongDocQA validation problem instances are evaluated on the same schedule but do not enter checkpoint selection. The selected update is update 70. Main-paper Table 7 reports the separate post-selection greedy evaluations of the base and trained participant policies.

G.3.3 Communication Diagnostics

Final-decision completion records whether an episode produces a final decision. “Every participant sends a message” records whether every participant appears at least once as a public-message sender. Participant coverage is the number of distinct public-message senders divided by team size, and the number of unique speakers is its unnormalized counterpart. Self-handoff rate is the fraction of valid handoffs in which the current speaker selects itself as the next participant. These diagnostics use one greedy rollout per problem instance and retain valid public actions produced before an episode failure. None enters the training reward.

G.3.4 Separating the Communication Trajectory from the Final-Decision Policy

The cross-replay analysis separates the communication trajectory from the final-decision policy. It uses the 40 validation problem instances for which both the base and trained communication trajectories produce a final decision. For each trajectory, we freeze the communication transcript, the identity and assigned PIU of the participant making the final decision, and the final-decision prompt, then regenerate the final decision with both the base and trained participant policies.

Let YB​BY_{BB}, YB​TY_{BT}, YT​BY_{TB}, and YT​TY_{TT} denote the scores from crossing the base and trained communication trajectories with the base and trained final-decision policies. We define the communication-trajectory effect as

12​[(YT​B−YB​B)+(YT​T−YB​T)]\frac{1}{2}\big[(Y_{TB}-Y_{BB})+(Y_{TT}-Y_{BT})\big]

and the final-decision-policy effect as

12​[(YB​T−YB​B)+(YT​T−YT​B)].\frac{1}{2}\big[(Y_{BT}-Y_{BB})+(Y_{TT}-Y_{TB})\big].

Intervals are percentile 95% intervals from 100,000 paired problem-instance-bootstrap samples.

On validation, the communication-trajectory effect is 6.95 points with a 95% interval of [0.49,13.78][0.49,13.78]. The final-decision-policy effect is −0.20-0.20 points with an interval of [−0.99,0.61][-0.99,0.61], and is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The cross-replay cell means represent policy-conditioned regenerated decisions rather than deterministic reproductions of the original final-decision strings.

G.3.4.1 Illustrative trajectory pair.

In one three-participant FinLongDocQA validation example, the base trajectory exhausts all 15 rounds, contains seven self-handoffs, and uses an incorrect flooring amount; both final-decision policies score 35% on that transcript. The trained trajectory contains no self-handoffs, voluntarily ends communication, and recovers the relevant amounts; both final-decision policies score 100%. This example illustrates how a changed communication trajectory can improve the decision while holding the final-decision policy fixed.

G.3.5 Additional Analysis of the Communication Trajectories

The completion-conditioned cross-replay excludes problem instances for which either original trajectory does not produce a final decision. We therefore run a second analysis on all 39 paired FinDVer validation problem instances and all 40 paired FinLongDocQA test problem instances. One GPT-5.5 final-decision policy receives the task and the valid communication transcript from each base and trained trajectory. It does not receive the original final decision, the participants’ assigned PIUs, original score, or an indication of which policy produced the transcript. All incomplete episodes end after an invalid participant response; for these, the input ends with the last valid public message. We evaluate the resulting decision with the same LLM-judged score used in the original evaluation.

We separately show GPT-5.4 the task, reference answer, answer components, reference PIUs, and communication transcript, without the policy identity, original final decision, or original score. For every PIU, the evaluator records public messages that communicate it and separately records messages that communicate an incompatible value, unit, period, sign, or scope. It also records whether each answer component is fully supported by public messages. Exact repetition is computed directly after case-folding and whitespace normalization and does not use an evaluator.

For each measurement, the reported change is the mean within-problem-instance trained-minus-base difference. Percentile 95% intervals use 100,000 paired problem-instance bootstrap samples with seed 20260922. Under the same final-decision policy, the score changes by 12.6212.62 points on FinDVer ([4.38,21.59][4.38,21.59]) and by −4.78-4.78 points on FinLongDocQA test ([−17.75,8.20][-17.75,8.20]). On FinDVer, the increase in the proportion of PIUs appearing in the communication transcript is 15.915.9 points with an interval of [4.4,28.1][4.4,28.1], and the increase in fully supported answer components is 9.59.5 points with an interval of [0.4,19.2][0.4,19.2]. On FinLongDocQA test, the corresponding changes are 0.00.0 points ([−11.2,11.2][-11.2,11.2]) and −1.2-1.2 points ([−12.5,10.4][-12.5,10.4]). Exact repetition increases by 31.931.9 points ([21.7,42.1][21.7,42.1]) on FinDVer and 25.525.5 points ([16.2,34.3][16.2,34.3]) on FinLongDocQA test.
